Propagating the initial wavenumber spectrum through the dispersion relation reproduces the retained fraction of angular momentum deficit across the full range of perturbation widths with no adjustable parameters. The confined perturbation is flanked by an apsidally polarized (oppositely-aligned) response, which we show to be the real-space imprint of this spectral projection. The softening length therefore sets a dynamical scale below which eccentricity perturbations spread only on timescales far longer than the secular period.

title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
abstract: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.

title: First Results of Calculation of the Dayside Magnetopause Reconnection Rate with TRACERS
abstract: Quantifying the rate of reconnection remains a key challenge in the study of geomagnetic storms. In this study, we present the first results from the new Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites (TRACERS) mission to calculate the reconnection rate from dispersed ion populations measured in the cusp, using previously developed methodology. We study ion dispersion events in two storms. During the first storm, which occurred on September 30, 2025, 21 dispersion events were identified in TRACERS 2 ion data as a combined result of geospace dynamics and the spacecraft cusp encounters. Throughout this time when ion dispersion was detected by TRACERS , the reconnection rate is calculated and is shown to track reasonably well with another measure of geomagnetic activity, the Cross Polar Cap Potential (CPCP) as obtained by the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN). The dispersions are correlated with the smoothed CPCP, and a correlation of $r^2=0.62$ was found using the dispersions from the onset and main phase of the storm. The correlation disappears when including dispersions from the recovery period. The distribution of reconnection rates throughout this storm lies generally between 0.1 - 1.5 mV/m, slightly lower than previous reconnection rates calculated with DMSP, but consistent with in-situ observations made with Polar. In this work, we also apply a previously developed automatic identification algorithm for ion-energy cusp dispersion to TRACERS, with the intent that it may serve as a tool for future statistical analysis as the data volume becomes too large to manually review.

title: Protegrity-PII Technical Report
abstract: We present Protegrity-PII, a new PII decision model for structured and unstructured text. Protegrity-PII achieves a typed recall of 0.915 with a precision of 0.907 on a new benchmark we propose, PII-SCOPE. Our model processes text in 0.49 seconds per million characters at \$0.0005 per million characters on a single RTX 6000 using batched inference. Due in part to the expansive nature of the entity type taxonomy used in training, Protegrity-PII achieves superior out-of-distribution generalization when benchmarked against a selection of state of the art models and datasets.

title: Unified Trajectory and 3D Pose Forecasting for Multi-Agent Sports Analysis
abstract: Forecasting future human motion requires jointly reasoning about an agent's global trajectory and 3D body pose, which are tightly coupled, particularly in team sports where multiple interacting players introduce complex social dynamics. We exploit a socio-temporal encoder that fuses trajectory and pose at the input level and models them jointly through shared factorized attention. The model is further enhanced by a per-joint loss reweighting scheme that emphasizes dynamic joints and prevents degenerate solutions, and a frequency-domain trajectory smoothing term that improves trajectory prediction while indirectly benefiting pose forecasting. To ensure fair comparison with prior joint forecasting methods, we identify and correct evaluation biases arising from overlapping sequence construction, adopting instead a non-overlapping protocol and a deterministic, oracle-free strategy for multi-future prediction. Our approach improves over prior joint forecasting methods on both WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains on pose accuracy, demonstrating that the proposed joint formulation generalizes beyond the densely interactive scenarios that motivate it.

title: NEST: Nested Embedding Representation for Multiscale Clustering
abstract: Real-world data often exhibits cluster structure at multiple resolutions, yet existing methods typically learn a single partition or construct an explicit hierarchy. Inspired by Matryoshka Representation Learning, we introduce NEST, an unsupervised framework that encodes coarse-to-fine structure within a single embedding. NEST jointly optimizes clustering and separation across nested prefix subspaces, enabling progressively finer distinctions as embedding dimensionality increases, with rank and within-cluster regularization that keep the embedding from collapsing. Empirically, distances in the learned embedding follow the hierarchy distance more closely than those of the input, although the hierarchy is never observed during training. On synthetic hierarchies, NEST recovers multiscale structure given only the number of clusters per level. Experiments on vision, text, and single-cell data further demonstrate multiscale organization across real-world representations. By making clustering granularity an intrinsic property of the representation, NEST provides a unified approach to multiscale structure discovery.

title: Drinfeld presentation of affine iquantum groups via iHopf algebras
abstract: Affine quantum groups $\widetilde{\mathbf{U}}$ and affine iquantum groups $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}^\imath$ admit two complementary descriptions: a Serre-type presentation and a Drinfeld (current) presentation. While iquantum groups $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}^\imath$ are typically defined via the Serre presentation, their Drinfeld presentations are substantially more subtle and less well understood. In this paper, we give a conceptual derivation of the Drinfeld presentation of $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}^\imath$ starting directly from the Drinfeld presentation of $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}$, working within the framework of iHopf algebras. This approach leads naturally to the definition of iquantum affinization associated with arbitrary Kac-Moody algebras $\mathfrak{g}$. We further show that, in this general setting, these iquantum affinizations can be realized as coideal subalgebras of quantum affinizations with respect to the Drinfeld coproduct. Finally, in the affine case, we describe the imaginary root vectors $Θ_{i,r}$ of $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}^\imath$ explicitly in terms of the root vectors $ψ^\pm_{i,r}$ of $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}$, thereby extending the results of Li and Przeździecki for certain affine types of $\widetilde{\mathbf {U}}^\imath$.

title: CREMA: Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms
abstract: The Collinear Resonance for Exotic Molecules and Atoms (CREMA) setup has been developed and commissioned at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Laboratory for Nuclear Science. The instrument combines the Doppler-suppressed resolution of the collinear fast-beam geometry with the selectivity of resonance ionization, for precision measurements of hyperfine structure and isotope shifts in atoms and molecules. We describe the setup, including the ion-optical simulations in which a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm provided the starting settings for the beam transport, and report commissioning measurements of the hyperfine structure of 133Cs. The extracted hyperfine constants agree with literature values within one standard deviation, demonstrating the operational readiness of the setup. CREMA mirrors the Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Experiment at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams and serves as its offline counterpart for the development of laser ionization schemes and techniques for future studies of exotic atoms and molecules.

title: A Study in Solution Models for SAT using the PBNF-transform
abstract: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described earlier in two articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a statement of conjunctions of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations, inverting the problem by \emph{multiplying} letters (literals) in the transferred clauses, now phrases: $pqrs\cdots s_{\ell}$, and using a binary iterated composition based on \emph{adding polynomials} for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value $1\mapsto 0$(T). To find a solution, we look for repeating literals in the clauses to factor out. With reversed literal repetition, we can even reduce the CNF to the sum of the transformed clauses.

title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
abstract: Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state-space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them---especially for nonlinear, high-dimensional systems---remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum-of-squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. These limitations have also shaped benchmark design: standard test suites are dominated by low-dimensional polynomial systems chosen to suit what solvers can handle rather than what engineering applications require. We address both sides of this challenge. First, we introduce DynaCertBench, a benchmark of 105 instances: 80 non-redundant systems curated from the literature, extended with high-dimensional and control-constrained variants and new nonlinearly coupled systems, comprehensively spanning stability, region-of-attraction, forward-invariance, and safety tasks. Second, we present LLM2Cert, an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes candidate certificates and verifies them against their proof obligations: each obligation is routed to an SMT solver or directly to the Lean Proof-Repair agent. On DynaCertBench, LLM2Cert verifies 81 of 105 instances ($77.1\%$), a $17.1$ percentage point improvement over one-shot proposal without feedback. On the 81 fixed certificates, LLM2Cert verifies 22 that All-SMT leaves unresolved. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/llm2cert.

title: TQFT gravity dual to the orbifold groupoid of Narain code CFTs over $\mathbb{Z}_4$
abstract: In a companion paper arXiv:2610.26610, we classified the Narain conformal field theories obtained by gluing copies of the $A_3$ root and weight lattices along their $\mathbb{Z}_4$ discriminant group. For two hyperbolic pairs, this gives twenty-two even self-dual gluing codes, which fall into seven inequivalent theories at $c=\bar c=6$. In this paper, we develop the physical interpretation of this family and its connections to three-dimensional topological field theory. We show that all twenty-two codes are topological boundary conditions of a single abelian Chern-Simons theory. Its invertible symmetries, which include fractional $B$-field shifts, organize the boundaries into three orbits: free, mixed and torsion. Boundaries in different orbits are related only by gauging. We determine all gaugings of order at most four between the seven theories, by $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $\mathbb{Z}_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$, with explicit twisted partition functions, and follow their effect on the spectrum and the current algebra. We then sum the Chern-Simons partition function over handlebodies at genus one and prove a finite Siegel-Weil identity, valid for any number of pairs. For two pairs, the handlebody sum is the uniform average over the free theories. Recovering the average over all twenty-two theories requires one additional contribution, a solid torus with the torsion lines along its core. For three or more pairs, we find that the handlebody sum is not a positive combination of code boundary states.

title: Localized Neutrinos in Two Dark Dimensions
abstract: We study neutrino masses in a six-dimensional framework with two compact dark dimensions. In the conventional flat-bulk realization, the sterile-neutrino zero mode is strongly volume suppressed, so a fundamental scale near $10~\mathrm{TeV}$ requires a large higher-dimensional Yukawa coupling to reproduce the observed neutrino masses, while the accompanying two-dimensional Kaluza--Klein tower is strongly constrained by oscillation data. We show that localizing the sterile-neutrino wave function near the Standard-Model brane substantially alleviates both effects. Using a Gaussian localizer, realistic Dirac neutrino masses are obtained with perturbative, order-one Yukawa couplings, while the brane-visible sterile excitations form a shell spectrum with $M_s^2=8μ^2 s$, and squared active--sterile mixings that decrease as $1/s$. The localization scale therefore separates the experimentally relevant sterile-neutrino spectrum from the gravitational compactification scale. We derive the resulting three-flavour structure and study its phenomenological consequences for reactor oscillations and tritium beta decay, including comparisons with current flat-LED and KATRIN constraints.

title: Austerity, Gender, and Multidimensional Deprivation Among Older Europeans: Evidence from SHARE
abstract: This paper studies whether fiscal consolidation is associated with deeper multidimensional deprivation among older women than among older men, and through which channel. Using six waves of SHARE across eleven European countries, it builds a multidimensional deprivation index spanning functional health, economic insecurity, and social exclusion, and relates it to the cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB) at the country-wave level in a two-way fixed-effects model. Consolidation raises deprivation on average with a null average gender gap, which is later found to conceal regional heterogeneity where the gender gap is positive and significant in Southern and Eastern Europe, and absent in Continental/Nordic Europe. This regional pattern holds under individual clustering but does not survive clustering at the country level. Further, the economic insecurity channel the literature would predict runs in the opposite direction, with men's measured insecurity rising more steeply than women's; this is the only dimension whose interaction survives country-level inference. Social exclusion exhibits a larger gender effect, concentrated in the Eastern and Southern Europe, but it is significant only under individual clustering. The gendered cost of austerity among older Europeans is therefore neither uniform across welfare regimes nor routed through income, though the evidence for its social channel is inconclusive.

title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.

title: Supercritical magnetic ray transforms in hyperbolic space: the complexification method from the transport-twistor lens
abstract: We present new inversion formulas for the unattenuated and attenuated magnetic ray transforms in the Poincaré disk, in the case of a constant, supercritical magnetic field. Our approach mirrors earlier complexification approaches by Novikov (Ark. Mat., 2002) and Bal (J. Math. Pures Appl., 2005), and a second feature of this article is to connect the approach with the Transport Twistor framework recently introduced by Bohr-Paternain (J. Éc. polytech. Math., 2023; arXiv:2606.25173).

title: The reverse Ritz inclusion: computable bounds on the pseudospectra of an operator by those of a finite-rank compression
abstract: We consider a bounded operator on a separable complex Hilbert space, reached only through its action on vectors and that of its adjoint, and split it along a subspace of finite dimension into a compression, a far block acting on the complement, and the two couplings between them. Given upper bounds on the norms of the couplings and of the far block, we show that outside a disc a pseudospectrum of the operator lies in a pseudospectrum of the compression, with an explicit loss in the level; this reverses the classical inclusion of the Ritz values in a pseudospectrum of the operator. The same bounds, with the smallest singular value of the shifted compression, bound the resolvent of the operator, count its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity inside every contour outside the disc on which a computed inequality holds, and enclose its spectral projector; no normality, self-adjointness or positivity is used.

title: Shorter but not more catalytic: an active-site-resolved model of how tau reshapes amyloid-$β$ secondary nucleation
abstract: Tau cross-seeding creates a mechanistic puzzle. Tau fibrils accelerate amyloid-$β$42 (A$β$42) nucleation and produce a larger population of shorter A$β$ fibrils, yet homotypic secondary nucleation occurs at rare catalytic sites rather than uniformly over fibril mass. Does making more, shorter fibrils make the A$β$ population more catalytic? A coupled tau-A$β$ model is extended to track fibril number, fibril mass, total active secondary-nucleation sites, and the fraction of sites exposed after plaque consolidation. The model recovers the preceding plaque-surface-limited formulation when active sites form in direct proportion to fibril mass. At matched fibril mass, shortening alone has little effect: the departure of active-site density from mass proportionality scales inversely with mean fibril size, so the extra fibrils matter only if each birth event introduces about as many sites as elongation adds over a mean-length fibril. At equal time, the sign of the homotypic response is controlled mainly by a Damkohler number comparing monomer consumption by elongation with monomer clearance. Tau coupling increases homotypic secondary nucleation while clearance controls free monomer, but suppresses it once elongation becomes the dominant monomer sink. In a composite scenario, these regimes occur in sequence. Across all cases examined, including 800 Latin-hypercube samples and simulations with mean fibril lengths of 0.3-30 $μm$, direct tau catalysis increases accumulated oligomer-equivalent exposure. The model predicts that shorter tau-seeded fibrils are not intrinsically more catalytic unless their sites are more numerous per unit mass, more active, or more exposed; matched-mass site counting and secondary-nucleation measurements can distinguish these alternatives.

title: Laser with $7\times10^{-18}$ stability
abstract: We report a laser with record frequency stability, based on a 21 cm cryogenic silicon cavity. For best short-term stability, the cavity operates at 6 K to minimize Brownian thermal noise and achieves a fractional stability of $7\times10^{-18}$ between 2 to 50 s of averaging time and 2.5 mHz linewidth. For best long-term stability the cavity operates at 16 K, where silicon has a zero-crossing of thermal expansion. Slightly increased thermal noise limits the performance to $9\times10^{-18}$, consistent with the expected temperature scaling, but the long-term performance is improved. The laser then has a linewidth of 2.9 mHz and long-term frequency drift less than 4 μHz s$^{-1}$. The laser is used to enhance the performance of a state-of-the-art Sr lattice clock, operating with Rabi and Ramsey interrogation times beyond 10 s.

title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

title: What if dark matter is composite of least interacting particles?
abstract: In this work, we investigate the possibility that Dark Matter contains particles that interact with known matter only through gravity, the least interacting particles (LIPs). Specifically, we consider the case of a dark Proca vector field, which does not mix in the kinetic term with any of the vector bosons of the Standard Model if a discrete symmetry (Z2 ) is imposed. Breaking this symmetry introduces kinetic mixing. Here, we study two realization mechanisms, namely kinetic mixing with the electromagnetic field after electroweak symmetry breaking (Scenario A) and kinetic mixing with the weak hypercharge gauge field (Scenario B). We also consider generalized kinetic terms that violate parity and time-reversal symmetries.

title: High-Order Fully Discrete Entropy-Stable DG Methods with Compact Explicit Single-Step Time Discretizations
abstract: We develop a unified framework for high-order, fully discrete entropy-stable discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods with compact explicit single-step time discretizations. At the end of each time step, the preliminary DG polynomial is scaled toward its cell average to enforce a strong cell entropy inequality while preserving conservation. This correction is feasible if and only if the updated cell average satisfies a weak cell entropy inequality, which standard third-order strong-stability-preserving Runge--Kutta DG updates can violate at arbitrarily small positive CFL numbers. For compact single-step schemes, including compact Runge--Kutta, Lax--Wendroff, and ADER-DG methods, we derive an explicit interval of feasible numerical entropy fluxes at each interface and prove that it is nonempty under a CFL condition. Projecting a compatible high-order target flux onto this interval guarantees the weak cell entropy inequality and preserves single-step high-order accuracy on smooth solutions, including near nondegenerate extrema. The limiter also enforces multiple entropy inequalities simultaneously. We also establish a Lax--Wendroff-type theorem. Numerical experiments for scalar conservation laws and the compressible Euler equations demonstrate high-order accuracy, multi-entropy control, and robustness for strong shocks.

title: Finite-width altermagnetic quantum rings: angular-channel hybridization and Aharonov--Bohm physics
abstract: We study a finite-width two-dimensional quantum ring with a quadratic $d$-wave altermagnetic term, Tan--Inkson confinement, a perpendicular magnetic field, and independently tunable Aharonov--Bohm (AB) flux. The altermagnetic interaction mixes $m$ and $m\pm2$ angular channels while preserving their parity. Circular symmetry renders the crystal orientation spectrally irrelevant and makes the two spin blocks exactly isospectral. The resulting same-parity anticrossings are resolved at low filling, and multichannel mixing is found near the Fermi level of highly occupied rings. Independent converged calculations for $N_e=1400$ and $1800$ establish the reconstructed Fermi edge and magnetic response in a finite field window and the persistent current over a full AB flux period. The analytic conventional reference separates radial-subband depopulation (dHvA-type cycles) from finer finite-ring shell oscillations; we do not assign a global Fourier spectrum to unverified altermagnetic field scans. The few-electron thermal response is obtained from an exact fixed-particle-number canonical partition function, avoiding finite-system errors of a fixed-mean-number approximation. The circular model supports an equilibrium charge current but no persistent spin current.

title: PLE: Physical-Engineering's Last Exam
abstract: Frontier language models now score above 90% on popular knowledge benchmarks and are increasingly deployed as agents that carry out multi-hour professional work. Yet no existing benchmark tests whether they can perform the real-world, economically valuable work of a professional physical engineer, such as modelling physics and legal code requirements across a multi-format project corpus, optimising material and installation costs, and issuing 2D/3D engineering design packages that a licensed reviewer would sign off on. Existing engineering benchmarks focus on textbook question answering, isolated tool calls or self-contained toy design problems. As a result, most of these benchmarks are already saturated by leading agents and solving them is far away from delivering real engineering design. We introduce PLE, a benchmark of 85 long-horizon, agentic tasks in professional physical engineering consisting of electrical, civil, structural and mechanical engineering, where solving a task means completing a realistic, billable engineering deliverable. PLE combines two complementary curation paths. Expert-Authored tasks are created end to end by practising engineers from a professional data provider's expert pool. Co-Authored tasks start from problem statements written by practising engineers; an adversarial Creator-Solver agent pipeline constructs each task's realistic project environment, executable grader and reference deliverables before sending them to expert engineers for validation and difficulty intensification. We evaluate a variety of frontier LLMs under seven publicly available agent harnesses. Even the strongest configuration reaches a mean score of only 50.6%, while spending 27M tokens and 63 minutes per task on average, demonstrating the substantial gap between current agents and autonomous physical engineering design.

title: Matrix Triangle Inequalities: Past, Present, and Future
abstract: This survey provides a concise overview of matrix triangle inequalities. Classical topics, such as inequalities for unitarily invariant norms, are revisited from a different perspective, with a particular emphasis on unitary orbit inequalities and various notions of matrix moduli. The exposition progresses from elementary results to much more recent developments, highlighting the evolution of the subject and its ongoing directions of research.

title: Dynamics of the Liquidity Profile in Concentrated Liquidity Provision: An SPIDE Approach
abstract: We model the dynamics of the liquidity profile in Uniswap~V3 and other concentrated-liquidity automated market makers with a stochastic partial integro-differential equation (SPIDE). The profile, the aggregate of all provider positions across tick space, evolves under a degenerate Sturm--Liouville operator, which encodes mean-reverting concentration around the market price, coupled with a Hilbert--Schmidt integral operator, which captures nonlocal redistribution driven by provider repositioning. We establish existence and uniqueness of the mild solution in a weighted $L^2$ space built on the Gegenbauer eigensystem, and reduce the SPIDE to a coupled system of linear stochastic differential equations whose low-order modes describe the level, slope, and curvature of the profile. Pairing the SPIDE with a log-price process yields tractable expressions for pool reserves, pool value, and loss-versus-rebalancing under Ornstein--Uhlenbeck-type and Black--Scholes-type noise. A finite-rank calibration in a fixed reference frame, applied to three Uniswap pools, gives interpretable estimates and lowers active-band forecast error relative to a martingale benchmark on the two pools compatible with the stationary specification. On the third pool, out-of-sample diagnostics are consistent with nonstationarity, which motivates price-aware and time-varying extensions.

title: Motion Retargeting with Spatiotemporal Preferences for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.

title: Damage detection in railway wheels from impact-induced ultrasonic ring-down using self-referenced decay features
abstract: This study evaluates a non-contact screening method for stationary railroad wheelsets using air-coupled ultrasonic measurements excited by hammer impacts. Two decay features are considered. First, an effective damping ratio is obtained by normalizing the measured decay rate by the dominant response frequency. Second, strike-to-strike variations are measured to assess the quality of the energy-decay fit for the overall wheel. The method was evaluated using 22 wheelsets at two railroad facilities. The analysis indicates that a random forest trained on one dataset and tested on another performed poorly. This result motivated a simpler approach based on thresholds applied to the two decay features, which fixed the feature definitions and calibrated the thresholds on either dataset. This approach correctly classified every wheelset in the other dataset. A more stringent wheel-level validation repeated second-feature selection and threshold calibration while each test wheelset was withheld. This procedure correctly classifies 21 of 22 wheelsets. All defective wheelsets are identified, while one healthy wheelset yields a false positive. The results further show that the two-feature detector transferred between the tested datasets for stationary assessment of wheel damage. Further evaluation is required using worn but serviceable wheels, controlled support conditions, and additional independent datasets.

title: Spin-Clifford Bundles and Spin Connections on the Hyperbolic Clifford Algebra - Part I
abstract: We develop the theory of spinor fields associated with the hyperbolic Clifford algebra $\mathbb{R}^{H}=\mathcal{C}\ell(H_V)$, which is associated with hyperbolic space $H_V=V\oplus V^{*}$. Algebraically, we exhibit an explicit real primitive idempotent which, unlike the Lorentzian case, remains primitive after complexification and generates the ideal of Witten superfields. We also describe the chirality decomposition and the hyperbolic spin group. Geometrically, we construct a canonical hyperbolic spin structure on every oriented manifold, showing that no topological obstructions arise beyond orientability and we study the associated spinor bundles, spin-Clifford bundles and ideal spinor subbundles. Finally, we introduce the isotropic extension of an arbitrary linear connection to $TM\oplus T^*M$, which is always compatible with the hyperbolic metric, and the associated hyperbolic spin connection, whose well-definedness, compatibilities, curvature and explicit form are established, providing the geometric framework for Dirac operators on the hyperbolic Clifford algebra, which we will present in a forthcoming article.

title: Rigid and $τ$-locally free modules via Taft algebras
abstract: We show that rigid modules are $τ$-locally free for a large family of 1-Iwanaga--Gorenstein algebras. This family includes many cases of the algebras introduced by Geiss--Leclerc--Schröer in their Inventiones paper "Quivers with relations for symmetrizable Cartan matrices I: Foundations", hence answering a question posed by Geiss--Leclerc--Schröer for many new cases. Our result is achieved by introducing coactions of Taft algebras and applying the recent theory developed by the first-named author and Coulembier.

title: Journal Basket: Supporting Cross-Disciplinary Literature Searching and Methodological Transparency
abstract: Business students beginning a research project must learn how to identify relevant scholarly publications, distinguish disciplinary sources, construct database searches, and report the decisions behind their literature reviews. These tasks can be difficult because journal classification systems and bibliographic databases organize scholarly information differently. This paper introduces Journal Basket, a browser-based tool developed to help business students conduct journal-bounded literature searches and currently available in beta. Journal Basket enables users to construct journal collections from the Australian Business Deans Council (ABDC) Journal Quality List, choose from 42 business discipline presets, entire ABDC fields or the Financial Times FT50 list, apply journal rating thresholds, and generate search expressions for Scopus, Web of Science and Business Source. Users can also inspect and modify journal collections, download journal inventories, and generate methodological descriptions and deterministic identifiers for journal selections. Companion learning resources use explanations, examples and interactive activities to teach review methods, database choice, referencing and the use of contemporary AI tools. Drawing on the journal-basket concept used by Litbaskets.io, I describe the educational motivation, design rationale, technical architecture, and practical workflow of Journal Basket. I distinguish reproducing a journal collection from reproducing an entire database search and discuss the limitations of journal rankings as search boundaries. The paper addresses scholarly information retrieval through a workflow for defining journal boundaries, generating database-specific queries and documenting search decisions.

title: Using Finite-Time Control to Synthesize Dynamic Backup Control Barrier Functions
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for the construction of control barrier functions (CBFs) for controllable linear systems subject to multiple state and input constraints. The approach is based on the Dynamic Backup CBF (DB-CBF) framework, where the control policy is parametrized using the equilibrium subspace of the system. By using a minimum-energy finite-time controller, we show that the terminal set constraint trivially reduces to having an admissible equilibrium point. The proposed DB-CBF is easy to tune (one parameter), fully takes advantage of the input range (by minimizing the control effort), and guarantees constraint enforcement (by tracking a backup equilibrium point that can be reached safely in finite time).

title: Very tight embeddings of subspaces of \(L_p\) for \(0<p<1\)
abstract: For \(0<p<1\) and \(μ>1\), every \(d\)-dimensional subspace of \(L_p\) embeds linearly into \(\ell_p^{\lfloorμd\rfloor}\) with distortion at most \(C(p,μ)(\log(d+2))^{1/p}\). If its Rademacher type \(q\) constant is at most \(T\), where \(p<q\leq2\), the distortion is at most \(C(p,q,μ)T\), independently of \(d\). We also give explicit bounds as \(μ\downarrow1\). This answers the question of Johnson and Schechtman concerning the extension of their very tight embedding theorem below exponent one. The proof combines compression at a lower exponent with a change of density that preserves the number of coordinates, and applies over both scalar fields.

title: Anisotropic thermoelectric transport in the Sr2RuO4-Ru eutectic system
abstract: The Sr2RuO4-Ru eutectic system, in which metallic Ru inclusions are embedded in a Sr2RuO4 matrix, exhibits an enhanced superconducting onset temperature of about 3 K, known as the 3-K phase. Here we investigate the in-plane thermoelectric response of this eutectic system in the normal state and find a pronounced anisotropy in the thermopower for thermal gradients applied parallel and perpendicular to the Ru lamellae. To clarify its origin, we combine thermopower measurements with electronic-structure-based transport calculations and finite-element modeling of the local strain distribution generated by the thermal-expansion mismatch between Sr2RuO4 and Ru. The calculations show that uniaxial compression of Sr2RuO4 produces a sizable thermopower anisotropy through modification of the Fermi surfaces. When an idealized spatially inhomogeneous strain field around the Ru lamellae is included, the observed sign and qualitative magnitude of the anisotropy are reproduced more closely than in a simple unstrained two-component model. These results are consistent with a substantial contribution from strain-induced changes in the Sr2RuO4 electronic structure near the interfaces, although contributions from interfacial phase mixing and three-dimensional transport connectivity cannot be excluded.

title: Atlas: Making Sense of Long Horizon Agent Trajectories
abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

title: AI-Native Academia Should Build a Community Verification Layer
abstract: This paper argues that AI-native academia should build a Community Verification Layer: interoperable, policy-governed infrastructure that converts researchers' routine reading and checking into persistent, claim- and version-linked evidence, while routing scarce deeper verification toward uncertain, consequential, and neglected research. AI is lowering the cost of producing plausible research artifacts faster than the cost of accountable evaluation, yet much of the evaluation researchers already perform while reading, citing, implementing, or extending work is never made reusable. We propose a tiered ladder from comprehension notes to claim checks, audits, artifact execution, reproduction, replication, and downstream validation. The layer would elicit judgments before revealing social signals, preserve multidimensional disagreement, privately verify contributors while allowing flexible public disclosure, allocate attention under expertise and coverage constraints, and make verification labor citable, with credit tied to the quality and depth of the evidence. We distinguish this design from prior open and post-publication review and outline governance requirements and potential counterarguments.

title: Thouless Pumping of One-Dimensional Dark Solitons and Domain Walls
abstract: We predict that quantized transport of dark solitons and domain walls can be observed in mutually sliding optical lattices in both focusing and defocusing nonlinear materials. Two different classes of underlying periodic backgrounds are considered here -- unstaggered and staggered -- which are accurately represented, respectively, by the in-phase and out-of-phase trains of Wannier functions. The nonlinear excitations formed on top of these backgrounds -- dark solitons and domain walls -- are sustained by defocusing or focusing Kerr nonlinearities of the optical medium. Despite non-zero asymptotics, dark solitons and domain walls can still undergo quantized topological transport in dynamically changing refractive index landscape when they and background on which they are constructed are dynamically stable. The extended intervals of propagation constants (and, correspondingly, of the background amplitude) and lattice depths, where stable quantized transport occurs, are identified for both dark solitons and domain walls. Outside these intervals, the quantized transport regime is found to be unstable. Our results extend the concept of nonlinear topological transport from bright to dark soliton states.

title: OMRC: Multipath Reliability for Direct-Connect Optical Interconnects
abstract: Network failures degrade Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC) in direct-connect optical datacenters. We propose Optical MRC (OMRC), which remaps collectives and circuits, preserving 95.7% of training throughput, restoring stalled inference, and achieving 4.7x MRC's simulated bandwidth.

title: Repair Changes Which Layers to Remove: Exact Optima for Depth Pruning of Language Models
abstract: Depth pruning removes entire transformer layers to make large language models faster, and recent methods recover quality by replacing the removed layers with a training-free linear map. Which layers to remove, however, is chosen with heuristic scores whose distance from the best choice is unknown. We evaluate every subset of layer groups exactly (about 53,000 pruned models across four families, with and without repair) and find that the best layers to remove depend on the repair: linear repair absorbs the interaction among nearby layers and turns the optimum from a split layout into a contiguous block, so methods that choose layers without the repair miss the repaired optimum by up to 189%. We therefore select layers under the repair that will be applied. A greedy search at the cost of SLEB lowers perplexity by 20% to 66% relative to ReplaceMe on five models up to 27B parameters, and with a task objective it is up to 25 points more accurate given the same data. A second-order expansion of the loss yields a score that selects the repaired block from one forward and one backward pass of the intact model.

title: Localizing Restriction Categories
abstract: The localizing/separating factorization, which is the analogue, for restriction categories, to the surjective/embedding factorization for topoi, is developed at both the mere restriction category and join restriction category level. The factorization system at both the ordinary and join level is approached using the notion of a density, which is a stable and universal suborder of the restriction order. The main technical results of the paper construct the join localization and establish its basic properties. The paper gives several examples of localizations. In particular, examples of localization on commutative rigs are provided which give a way to construct categories of schemes. The Zariski spectrum and the Pierce spectrum are, in particular, developed.

title: Return Time Sets of Minimal Points for Countable Group Actions
abstract: For a countably infinite discrete group $G$, we study subsets of $G$ that contain a neighbourhood return-time set of a minimal point in a $G$-flow $X$. For $e\in F\subseteq G$, we characterize this property by the existence of $e\in A\subseteq F$ such that $\operatorname{Int}_K(A):=\{t\in G:Kt\subseteq A\}$ is right syndetic for every finite $K\subseteq A$, and equivalently by the support of a minimal binary configuration in the Bernoulli shift $2^G$. Additional conditions on $\operatorname{Int}_K(A) \operatorname{Int}_K(A)^{-1}$ characterize realization by minimal flows that are weakly mixing of all finite orders or strongly mixing: for every such $K$, the former requires that for each finite $H\subseteq G$ there is $c\in G$ with $HcH\subseteq \operatorname{Int}_K(A) \operatorname{Int}_K(A) ^{-1}$, whereas the latter requires that $\operatorname{Int}_K(A)\operatorname{Int}_K(A)^{-1}$ be cofinite. We also construct, for every compact metrizable minimal $G$-flow, a free minimal, strongly mixing Cantor flow disjoint from it.

title: Probing quasiperiodic spectral accessibility with a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle
abstract: Quasiperiodic systems combine sharply different spectral and localisation regimes with a dense hierarchy of dynamical time scales. We show that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can use this structure as a thermodynamic probe, revealing which parts of the spectrum become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant during a driven transformation. For a generalised Aubry-André-Harper chain, the resulting response is not determined by the static quasiperiodic regime alone: extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols do not exhibit universal ordering of work fluctuations. Instead, the statistics reflect transition pathways that are simultaneously dynamically coupled, thermally occupied, and energetically significant. The same spectral accessibility separates thermodynamic recovery from microscopic adiabatic recovery. Positive mean work can reappear while the population transfer dynamics remain strongly nonadiabatic because finite-rate population transfer is redistributed toward energetically less costly channels rather than suppressed. The full work distribution reveals a further separation, with a finite rate window in which positive-work cycles form a majority although the mean work remains negative. This behaviour persists in finite-size analysis. A thermally weighted spectral susceptibility connects these effects to a distributed hierarchy of dynamically active spectral regions rather than to a single minimum-gap bottleneck. Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture while introducing a second time scale and intercycle memory. Quantum Otto cycles can therefore provide a fluctuation-resolved thermodynamic probe of quasiperiodic spectral accessibility, complementary to direct spectroscopic and eigenstate-resolved diagnostics.

title: Field-free superconducting diode and tunable vortex dynamics in NbN/FePt stripe-domain heterostructures
abstract: We demonstrate reconfigurable, field-free superconducting diode behavior in NbN/FePt and NbN/AlN/FePt heterostructures with remanent stripe domains in the FePt layer. NbN films 10 nm thick are capped either directly with FePt or through a thin AlN spacer, which reduces electronic proximity effects while preserving magnetic coupling through stray fields. At zero applied magnetic field, the superconducting diode efficiency reaches approximately 50--60% in NbN/FePt when the stripes are perpendicular to the current and is strongly reduced when they are parallel. The diode effect persists in NbN/AlN/FePt with efficiencies reaching approximately 35--40%, supporting a magnetic origin of the nonreciprocity. We interpret the response as asymmetric vortex transport in the remanent magnetic landscape, with preferential edge vorticity and a Lorentz force that favors inward flux injection or outward motion depending on current polarity. Under applied perpendicular magnetic fields, the interplay between the external field and the magnetic stray fields modifies the flux-flow instability and the apparent instability velocity inferred from transport, with values below those reported for bare NbN films. These results show that stripe-domain ferromagnetic overlayers provide a reconfigurable route to control superconducting nonreciprocity and flux-flow stability in NbN-based heterostructures.

title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent

title: Multiplicity Distribution in the Color Glass Condensate Formalism
abstract: The multiplicity distribution (MD) of charged particles in high-energy proton-proton collisions remains an intricate aspect of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Traditional models, such as the Negative Binomial Distribution (NBD), were fitted and successfully described MDs at lower energies, but fail at higher energies, such as those probed by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), where a ``shoulder-like'' structure emerges. To address this, we employ the Double Negative Binomial Distribution (DNBD), a weighted combination of two NBDs, representing contributions from soft and semi-hard processes. This model typically involves six free parameters, but by incorporating the $k_T$ factorization formalism and introducing an energy scale $Λ$, we effectively reduce the number of free parameters from six to four while maintaining a strong fit to high-energy MD data. The unintegrated gluon distribution used in this work is derived from the Golec-Biernat-Wüsthoff (GBW) model. Additionally, we investigate the KNO scaling and use the $k_T$ factorization formalism to describe the pseudo-rapidity distribution. Our approach demonstrates excellent agreement with recent experimental data, yielding low $χ^2$ values and highlighting the potential for improvements using more realistic gluon distribution model. This analysis provides valuable insights into the interplay of soft and semi-hard processes in high-energy collisions.

title: Exact Characterization of Admissible Bandwidths for Linear Disturbance Observers
abstract: This paper characterizes the entire set of admissible Q-filter bandwidths, equivalently parameterized by the time constant $τ$, that guarantee robust internal stability of a linear disturbance observer (DOB) under parametric plant uncertainties. Classical small-$τ$ stability results provide a rigorous foundation for Q-filter bandwidth design. Building on this foundation, we formulate the $τ$-dependent robust internal-stability problem as a semialgebraic feasibility problem in bivariate polynomials and prove that the complete admissible set is a finite union of open intervals under the standing assumptions. A constructive procedure with exact membership tests recovers all stabilizing intervals. A numerical example with an uncertain plant family containing non-minimum-phase members illustrates a disconnected admissible set.

title: Rematching Estimators for Average Treatment Effects
abstract: Matching estimators are widely applied in practice for their great intuitive appeal. However, simple matching estimators with a fixed number of matches ($M_0$) are generally inefficient. In this article, we propose matching estimators with a variable number of matches to gain efficiency via rematching. Rather than increasing $M_0$ to gain precision, which introduces an increase in bias, the key is to rematch the treated units from the opposite direction to utilize unmatched control units. Our rematching estimators are applicable to both the average treatment effect and its counterpart for the treated population. The proposed rematching estimators are proven asymptotically valid and uniformly more efficient than matching estimators with the same $M_0$. Simulation results confirm that the proposed rematching estimators substantially improve the simple matching estimators in finite samples. As an empirical illustration, we apply the estimators proposed in this article to the National Supported Work data.

title: Classification of binary, ternary and quaternary Hermitian LCD codes
abstract: We extend the complete classifications of linear complementary dual (LCD) codes from length 15 to length 19 in the binary case, from length 10 to length 15 in the ternary case and from length 12 to length 13 in the quaternary Hermitian case. The classification rests on a reduction of the monomial equivalence of LCD codes to graph isomorphism on the coordinates, combined with canonical augmentation.

title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
abstract: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.

title: Selling Evidence Bit by Bit
abstract: We study the sale of an asset to competitive buyers. Before the sale, the seller can buy hard information about the asset from an intermediary who designs and prices a test to maximize his revenue guarantee across equilibria. The test consists of one or more signals, and the seller privately chooses which subset of signals to buy and selectively discloses their realization to the buyers. We show that the intermediary benefits from splitting information into multiple signals and characterize his maximal revenue guarantee as the cumulative entropy of the asset value distribution. This guarantee is achieved by a sequence of ``skim from the top'' tests with binary, i.i.d.\ signals and additive pricing. Furthermore, any sequence of tests that achieves the maximal guarantee reveals the asset's value in the limit. For binary values, we also characterize the revenue guarantee for any given number of signals, and show that it is achieved by a test that corresponds to a ``Swiss cheese" model of failure with conclusive good news.

title: When News Gets Old: Portfolio Allocation with Reinforcement Learning and Large Language Models
abstract: Financial news can influence investment decisions long after publication. Timely news may reach an investor before prices fully adjust, whereas older news may already be reflected in prices. We examine two ways to handle aging signals: retain them and give a portfolio policy timing information, or filter them out before portfolio selection. A fixed large language model (LLM) extracts signals from public SEC disclosures. We compare these treatments in reinforcement learning (RL) policies and LLMs that choose portfolios directly. We evaluate returns after trading costs in historical tests over 2023-2025. RL choices respond to timing information in a controlled test, but historical returns show no consistent benefit from adding it. For the LLM, filtering old news produced the highest average net return, reaching 18.43% per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks. This exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.

title: Computable presentations of separable Lebesgue spaces
abstract: For every right-c.e.\ real $p\in(1,2)$, $L^p[0,1]$ has a computable presentation. The proof combines an effective stability modulus for almost isometric embeddings with a Fra\"ıssé-style construction in which the exponent varies. In the same range, if $\ell^p$ has a computable presentation, then $p$ is computable. Combining these with the known results gives the computable presentability classification for all separable Lebesgue spaces. We also formulate an effective Fra\"ıssé theorem for Banach spaces and apply it to obtain a computable presentation of the Gurarij Banach space.

title: Learning-Oriented Fault-Tolerant Control for UAVs with Time-Varying Fault Estimation
abstract: The increasing deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in safety-critical applications has created a growing demand for control strategies that remain reliable in the presence of actuator and sensor faults. This paper presents a fault-tolerant control framework that combines constructive mathematical modeling, proportional--integral (PI) fault estimation, and learning-oriented control. A nonlinear quadcopter model is first developed using both the Newton--Euler and Euler--Lagrange formulations, from which a discrete-time linear model is derived for observer and controller design. A PI observer is then proposed to estimate actuator and sensor faults, with exponential estimation-error convergence established for constant faults in the absence of disturbances and ultimate boundedness established for slowly time-varying faults under bounded disturbances. The estimated fault signals are incorporated into an active fault-tolerant control architecture together with a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) controller, which is trained using only the yaw channel and subsequently applied to improve closed-loop tracking performance. Numerical simulations illustrate the observer's estimation performance under constant and slowly time-varying faults, including bounded disturbances, and the tracking performance of the integrated controller under multiple actuator and sensor fault scenarios. The proposed framework combines model-based fault estimation with learning-based control to improve fault accommodation and tracking performance in UAV systems.

title: Collinear motions in constant curvature spaces, and coplanar motions in $\mathbb{R^4}$
abstract: A collinear motion of an $n$-body problem is one in which the $n$-bodies always lie along some, possibly moving, geodesic during their evolution. We prove that every collinear motion of $n\geq 3$ bodies in a constant non-zero curvature space is necessarily contained in some fixed constant curvature space of dimension at most three. For natural systems admitting energy and angular momentum integrals, we further show that every such motion is necessarily a relative equilibrium: evolving under uniform rotation while maintaining constant mutual distances. These results extend certain classical results on collinear motions in Euclidean spaces, initiated by P. Pizzetti, to general spaces of constant curvature. The same methods also yield a partial answer to a question of A. Wintner. Namely, we show that any concave and always coplanar motion in the Euclidean 4-body problem, where the moving plane containing the bodies sweeps out an $\mathbb{R}^4$, must be self-similar: maintaining constant mutual distance ratios over the motion.

title: Beyond Better Ideas: How Human-AI Collaboration Shapes Scientific Ideas and Human Perceptions
abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.

title: Non-aware computable presentations of randomizations
abstract: Let 2 be the two-element structure in the empty signature. We build a computable presentation Q of the Borel randomization $2^{[0,1)}$ in which neither constant random variable is a computable point. Consequently, Q is not aware. This gives a negative answer to a question of Cuervo Ovalle and Goldbring \cite{CG}. We also construct a countable structure $M$ with no computable presentation but $M^{[0,1)}$ has a computable presentation. This answers another question and establishes the necessity of the awareness condition stated in one of the main theorems in \cite{CG}.

title: Rest-frame Ultraviolet Variability of Quasars in the Cosmic Himalayas Overdensity
abstract: Some high-redshift overdensities show an enhanced incidence of AGNs, suggesting that large-scale environment may influence supermassive black hole fuelling and triggering. Whether environment also affects AGN variability remains unclear.Using the Cosmic Himalayas (CH), an extreme concentration of 11 type 1 quasars at z=2.16-2.20, we investigate possible offsets in rest-frame ultraviolet variability relative to quasars with comparable redshifts, black hole masses, and Eddington ratios.We construct a parent sample of 1,138 Stripe 82 quasars at 2.11<=z<=2.25 and combine photometry from the SDSS, the PS1, and the ZTF to build observer-frame g- and r-band light curves spanning up to 27~yr. We compare DRW parameters and ensemble structure functions (SFs) with control pseudo-samples matched in black hole mass and Eddington ratio, and use injection--recovery simulations to forecast the detectability of a CH-like offset.The CH quasars show a tendency toward shorter DRW damping timescales (median offsets of -0.32 and -0.13 dex in g and r) and slightly higher asymptotic amplitudes. None of the four DRW comparisons is statistically significant, including the largest offset in the g-band damping timescale (p=0.16). Ensemble SFs generally exceed matched-control medians, although 18 of 19 lag bins per band remain within the 95% pointwise envelopes. Assuming a true uniform -0.32 dex g-band timescale offset, injection--recovery simulations predict an 80% probability of nominal 3sigma detection with approximately 60 quasars of comparable variability scatter and data quality.If confirmed, the tentative variability offsets may suggest that large-scale environment influences accretion-flow variability beyond its potential role in quasar triggering. Larger samples with higher-precision light curves, such as those expected from the LSST, are required to test this possibility.

title: Stale Instruction Files Override the Code in Coding Agents: A One-Sentence Fix
abstract: Purpose: Coding agents follow a project's instruction file, such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, even when it disagrees with the existing code and even when they notice the disagreement. We measure this behaviour and test whether one sentence in the user's own instruction file makes agents follow the code instead. Methods: We built 40 Python projects in which the instruction file asks for one convention while the existing code uses another, for example print instead of logging. Claude Code and Codex CLI added a feature to each project, with and without a sentence in the user-level instruction file that gives the existing code precedence, in 320 runs. Results: Without the sentence, 90.1% of the agents' choices followed the stale file. Claude Code pointed out the conflict in 79 of 80 runs and still followed the file. Codex CLI rewrote the existing code to match the file in 20 of 80 runs, and the project's own tests then failed in 17 of them. The sentence raised the share of choices that follow the code from 4.2% to 91.4%, stopped the rewrites and raised the test pass rate from 89.4% to 100%. Conclusion: We attribute the behaviour to how agents receive the two sources: the instruction file reaches the model as an instruction and the code as tool output, which models are trained to rank lower. Users can add the sentence today, and makers of agents and models can build the same rule into their products.

title: Beyond the Fock Vacuum in Finite-$N$ Bilocal Algebras of Vector Models
abstract: We discuss the finite-$N$ Hilbert space of bilocal operators that underlies bilocal holography of vector models, beyond the sector built on the Fock vacuum. If the microscopic oscillator Fock space carries a multiplicity-free dual action of a compact color group $G$ and a bilocal algebra, Howe duality implies that projection to the derived subgroup $[G,G]$ selects precisely the characters of the abelianization $G^{\rm ab}=G/[G,G]$ that occur in the Fock space. Thus $O(N)/SO(N)=\mathbb Z_2$ gives two sectors, $U(N)/SU(N)=U(1)$ gives integer determinant-charge sectors, while $Sp(N)$ is perfect and gives no additional sector; Bose/Fermi statistics and the number of modes determine which sectors are actually realized. We construct the epsilon and determinant backgrounds that generate these sectors, together with their finite-$N$ constraints and Casimirs, and find that the two bosonic $O(N)$ sectors are not distinguished by any Casimir. Using group-integral projectors, we derive explicit sector-resolved characters for the $O(N)$ and $U(N)$ theories. Around each new background we solve the constraints with auxiliary oscillators, which form a Fermi sea for bosonic matter. In the free vector model on $\mathbb R\times S^2$ the new sectors consist of baryonic primaries; we determine their energies, degeneracies and spin content exactly at finite $N$, together with their lowest energy at fixed angular momentum.

title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
abstract: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non-personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag-Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench.

title: Asymptotics of local height pairing without Hodge conjecture
abstract: We remove the assumption of the Hodge conjecture from the asymptotic formula for the Archimedean local height established in our previous work. We also remove other minor assumptions. We achieve this by exploiting the cohomological nature of Beilinson's local intersection index rather than arguing motivically.

title: Scattering theory for bulk and surface waves in an impedance half-space, II: local perturbations, the scattering matrix and an inverse problem
abstract: We study the Robin, or impedance, Laplacian on a half-space of dimension $n \ge 3$ which is perturbed inside a fixed ball. The boundary may be deformed, and obstacles may be present in the interior or attached to the boundary, in any combination and with no smallness assumption. Outside the ball the configuration is the flat impedance half-space of Part I, with constant impedance $α> 0$, where a bulk channel and a surface channel propagate at every positive energy and only the surface channel propagates on the band $(-α^2,0)$. We prove a limiting absorption principle, valid at every positive energy and outside a discrete set of embedded eigenvalues in the band. We construct the generalized Fourier transform and prove its completeness by a stationary argument which constructs no wave operator and reduces completeness to the uniqueness of the scattering solution at each energy. We then obtain the scattering matrix, its unitarity and a two-channel optical theorem. The main result is a uniqueness theorem for the inverse problem. Under two geometric conditions on the pair, the scattering amplitude at a single positive energy determines the perturbation completely, and the argument does not distinguish a deformation of the boundary from an obstacle. It follows that no nontrivial perturbation satisfying the same conditions is invisible at any positive energy. On the surface band the corresponding statement is reduced to one explicitly stated question about the exterior Robin problem.

title: Bridging the Closed-World Gap: Interpretable Anomaly Detection via a Hybrid TSK-FCM Ensemble on the BETH Dataset
abstract: A fundamental paradox plagues the deployment of Machine Learning in cybersecurity: supervised models generalize poorly to novel, Out-of-Distribution (OoD) attacks, whereas unsupervised models often suffer from poor separability, leading to unmanageable false-alarm rates. This challenge is exemplified by the BETH dataset, a kernel-level benchmark in which the training data consists solely of benign and suspicious insider behaviors, whereas the test set consists almost entirely of novel botnet activation attacks. To bridge this detection gap, we propose a Hybrid Fuzzy Ensemble that synergizes the precision of supervised learning with the adaptability of unsupervised clustering. Our architecture integrates a gradient-optimized Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy classifier to act as an expert on known insider threats, with a parallel Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) module to detect geometric anomalies. A critical finding of our research is that traditional fuzzy membership scores degrade in high-dimensional feature spaces due to the curse of dimensionality. We overcome this by introducing a robust Min Distance metric that exploits the raw geometric isolation of botnet activation attacks. This approach yields a state-of-the-art AUROC of 0.9951 on the BETH test set, outperforming the original Isolation Forest baseline by 17.1%. By combining near-perfect OoD detection with the intrinsic interpretability of fuzzy logic, our framework offers a viable path toward robust, transparent, and autonomous network defense.

title: Evaluating Type-1 Diabetes Digital Twins by Decision Quality
abstract: A digital twin (DT) for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can predict how an individual's blood glucose will respond to different insulin treatments without actually trying them. For each treatment, downstream statistics of predicted glucose trajectories, such as glycemic risk, can be computed to guide clinical decisions. However, the quality of DTs is usually measured by the accuracy of their predicted glucose trajectories, which may not reflect the quality of the downstream treatment decisions they inform. In this work, we directly evaluate DTs by this decision quality on downstream treatment ranking, i.e., whether a DT predicts glucose trajectories that can be used to rank candidate treatments as the real patient would. We present an evaluation protocol over 30 virtual patients from the FDA-accepted UVA/Padova model, each simulated under 21 different basal-bolus treatments. For each patient, a DT is fitted under one treatment and then produces glucose trajectories for the remaining 20 treatments. Our results show that prediction accuracy and decision quality disagree. A baseline that models the average patient, never seeing the individual's glucose data, has the lowest prediction accuracy of all six methods (RMSE: 63.6 mg/dL) but ranks treatments with the second-highest mean Spearman (0.766), while a black-box neural network that predicts glucose nearly twice as accurately (RMSE: 32.9 mg/dL) ranks them no better than a random ordering of the 20 treatments (0.049 Spearman). Therefore, selecting a DT based on prediction accuracy alone can prefer one that recommends treatments at chance, and decision quality must be evaluated directly rather than assumed to follow from prediction accuracy.

title: Deep-Learning Identification and Global Characterization of Energetic O2+ Beams at Mars
