Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS survey: A Keplerian Circumbinary Disk Candidate in the High-mass Star-forming Region IRAS 08303-4303
abstract: We present the ALMA Band 6 continuum and molecular line observations of IRAS 08303-4303, a high-mass star-forming region, with an angular resolution of $\sim 0.3''$ ($\sim 700$ au at the distance of 2.35 kpc). Six dense condensations are identified in the 1.3 mm continuum, and at least four of them are associated with molecular outflows. The estimated outflow parameters, particularly mass outflow rates $\geq 10^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, suggest that the driving sources are high-mass young stellar objects. Two of the condensations are forming a wide protobinary system with a separation of $\sim 900$ au. They reside within a single rotating structure, identified as a circumbinary disk which has a mass of about 2 $M_{\odot}$. This structure is traced by multiple molecular lines and exhibits a Keplerian rotation pattern. Based on the Keplerian rotation assumption, the enclosed mass is derived to be between 32 and 61 $M_{\odot}$: 22-43 $M_{\odot}$ for the primary and 10-18 $M_{\odot}$ for the secondary. The circumbinary disk is on the whole gravitationally stable, yet some parts with Toomre $Q < 2$ indicate potential fragmentation. Various molecular lines reveal a streamer-like structure connecting to the circumbinary disk, suggesting transfer of material from the envelope to the protobinary system through it. Despite the observational rarity of such circumbinary disks around high-mass YSOs, the high binary fraction among massive stars underscores their significance. This source, therefore, serves as a key laboratory for understanding the formation of high-mass binary systems.

title: Constrain the number of inner horizons from gravitational Noether charges
abstract: A central question in the study of black hole interiors is how matter and geometry constrain the number of horizons. In Einstein gravity, one known method is to use the ADM decomposition of the field equations to derive a differential inequality for the lapse, which then constrains the possible multiple inner horizons. We show that the same obstruction can instead be formulated through the Komar integral as a bulk-boundary balance of gravitational Noether charge. In higher-curvature gravity, a direct ADM analysis becomes more complicated, whereas the gravitational Noether charge naturally retains this bulk-boundary structure. We naturally apply the gravitational Noether charge analysis to Lovelock gravity. We introduce a TCC-like curvature condition and prove that, together with the thermodynamically motivated assumption of positive Wald entropy, it allows at most one nondegenerate inner Killing horizon inside a nondegenerate event horizon. This suggests that the obstruction reflects a compatibility between bulk gravitational response and horizon thermodynamics.

title: Breaking the Coupling: Efficient Concurrency Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Data Race Detection
abstract: Detecting data races in the Linux kernel requires exploring both the input space and the thread-interleaving space. Existing kernel concurrency fuzzers couple these two searches by exploring interleavings during fuzzing, often spending substantial scheduling effort on inputs with little potential to trigger real races. In this paper, we present a new concurrency fuzzing paradigm that decouples concurrent-input generation from thread-interleaving exploration, enabling expensive scheduling to focus on promising inputs. To identify inputs that warrant targeted scheduling, we introduce May Race Pairs (MRPs), which represent conflicting memory-access pairs observed within a dynamically determined time threshold. Our framework first generates and executes concurrent syscall groups without controlled scheduling, collecting MRPs to guide further input mutation and identify schedule-worthy inputs. It then uses a separate scheduling instance to explore targeted interleavings and confirm real data races. To improve the effectiveness of both stages, we incorporate LLM-assisted semantic mutation for generating diverse syscall groups, backpressure-guided dynamic threshold control for balancing candidate production and scheduling consumption, and history-aware context recovery, context-aware interleaving scheduling, and candidate MRP prioritization for efficient race confirmation. We implement our framework for the Linux kernel and evaluate it on eight common kernel modules in Linux 6.17. It discovers 187 unique real-world data races, including 59 harmful races. Under the same testing budget, our approach detects substantially more data races than existing kernel concurrency fuzzers, including SegFuzz and CONZZER. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of decoupling concurrent-input generation from interleaving exploration and concentrating scheduling effort on promising candidates.

title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.

title: xVGAE: A Hierarchical Variational Graph Autoencoder for Exchangeable Graphs
abstract: Graphs play a crucial role in many applications, ranging from drug discovery to social network modeling and astronomy. Generative models for graphs have substantially advanced in recent years, but we identify relatively simple scenarios where state-of-the-art models struggle to converge within a standard compute budget, or exhibit prohibitively slow generation times. We propose a generative architecture that achieves quality competitive with state-of-the-art models and is orders of magnitude faster at generation. Our approach is inspired by the Aldous-Hoover theorem, a classic representation theorem that characterizes any probability distribution of graphs that is invariant to permutations of node indices or exchangeable. This theorem establishes that three ingredients suffice: a graph-level latent variable, a set of exchangeable node-specific latent variables, and a so-called graphon function that maps graph- and node-level variables to the probability of an edge between any node pair. Given a training set of graphs, our exchangeable Variational Graph AutoEncoder (xVGAE) learns an approximation to their underlying graphons, as well as graph- and node-level latent variables. We show that our xVGAE encodes latent representations that correlate with graph- and node-level properties, and can (quickly, in one shot) generate new graphs that closely match key training set statistics.

title: A recurring changing state AGN discovered in the SAMI Galaxy Survey and SDSS
abstract: We present a detailed analysis of the AGN in galaxy J085337.26+014303.6 at z=0.0582. A combination of SDSS and SAMI Galaxy Survey data shows that this object has gone through at least one full changing-look AGN cycle, from type 1.9 in 2001 to type 1 in 2015 and 2021, and then type 1.9 again in 2022. While the broad lines in this object show evidence of dust obscuration, detailed spectral analysis plus WISE photometry demonstrate that the changes in this object are related to a physical state change, not changing obscuration. In fact, the WISE light curve suggests that this object may have briefly returned to a type 1.9 state in 2020. In the optical, the host galaxy dominates the light (e.g. only ~10 per cent contribution from the AGN at 4000 Angstoms within a central aperture), even in the high state. In contrast, the brightest WISE W2-band measurements place the AGN at a similar luminosity to the entire host galaxy. The broad Balmer lines show evidence of multiple components, with a weak very-broad component (FWHM=5000-6000 km/s) visible in the low type 1.9 state, and a stronger broad component of FWHM~2000 km/s dominating in the high type 1 state. We propose that this is caused by two spatially distinct regions within the broad line region.

title: Robot Motion Transition with a Human Motion Prior
abstract: Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project

title: HC-AINet: An Auditory-Inspired Network with Harmonic Compensation for Low-Complexity Speech Enhancement
abstract: Speech enhancement on resource-constrained devices requires noise suppression with limited computation and minimal loss of spectral detail. Auditory-inspired subband processing reduces computation, but its smooth gains have limited ability to distinguish harmonic peaks from neighboring noise. We propose a harmonic-compensated auditory-inspired network (HC-AINet) for low-complexity speech enhancement. A triangular equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB) filterbank supplies compact features to a lightweight network comprising inverted-residual units, temporal Conformer layers, and parallel frequency-gated convolutions. The network predicts global and harmonic gains together with fusion weights. A harmonic-location map derived from the noisy spectrum confines the harmonic contribution to selected bins on the original frequency grid, while the global branch controls the broader spectral envelope. The compensated magnitude, noisy phase, and a magnitude-derived minimum-phase cue jointly condition a compact phase estimator for waveform reconstruction. On VoiceBank-DEMAND, the 64-band model achieves a PESQ of 3.20 and a STOI of 0.95 with approximately 0.27 million parameters.

title: TEAR: Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold authority. Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability profiles. We formulate this complementarity as a control authority routing problem and present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation (TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy. TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains consistent with the current task. A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to time authority transfers. Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8-27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30-40% over autonomy-only execution in our settings. These results demonstrate the potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human control.

title: Spatial Decay and Asymptotic Stability of Forced Waves at the Critical Speed for the Fisher-KPP Equation in a Shifting Environment
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the spatial decay and asymptotic stability of forced waves for the Fisher-KPP equation in a shifting heterogeneous environment, focusing on the critical speed $c_*=2\sqrt{r_+}$. Within the framework of regular variation, we establish a complete classification of critical wave tails in terms of the asymptotic behavior of the environmental deviation $r_+-r(z)$ as $z\to+\infty$. In each case, we derive precise spatial decay that characterize how the environmental tail modifies the leading-order decay of the wave at criticality. We further establish asymptotic stability estimates of forced waves. For initial data satisfying an exponentially weighted boundedness condition, we prove an $O(t^{-1/2})$ convergence rate in the uniform norm. Under stronger spatial decay assumptions on the weighted initial data, this rate improves to $O(t^{-1-σ/2})$, for $σ\in[0,1]$, in both the uniform norm and a weighted norm. Moreover, no smallness assumption on the initial perturbations is needed for our results.

title: An Approximate-Diagonal Characterization of Amenable Actions on C*Algebras
abstract: We introduce relative $h$-diagonals for crossed products $A\rtimes_αΓ$ by discrete groups, which are positive-form approximate diagonals in the Haagerup tensor product taken relative to $A$. We show that $α$ is amenable if and only if $A\rtimes_αΓ$ admits a relative $h$-diagonal, an analogue of Johnson's theorem for $L^{1}(G)$.

title: TESSA: A Governance-Oriented Custom GPT for SME Guidance under the EU AI Act: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
abstract: The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

title: Neural Spectral Capacity with Residual Context for Heterogeneous Resource Allocation within Transformers
abstract: Predicting relative trained performance from architectural specifications can guide design when training costs limit experimentation. Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) provides such a heuristic, but scores projections independently and assigns identical scores to compatible reorderings of the same layer configurations. We introduce Residual-Aware Neural Spectral Capacity (ResNSC) for Transformers, using a specification-derived statistical reference for accumulated residual updates to determine the input and residual-state statistics in each projection's capacity calculation, while retaining additive evaluation without data or instantiated weights. When residual widths vary, earlier choices affect later scores, so we augment NSC's allocator (NSC-DP) with residual history beyond its layer-and-budget state. ResNSC-DP jointly allocates residual and feed-forward widths under a resource budget, with certified bounds on the best numerically evaluated ResNSC score within a specified finite candidate set. At the 121M and 374M pretraining scales, selected architectures achieve lower mean perplexity than uniform, variable-width, and tapered allocations on FineWeb-Edu, WikiText-2, and LAMBADA at comparable parameter budgets. In inherited-weight LLaMA-7B pruning using the LoNAS supernet, ResNSC-DP improves eight-task average accuracy over NSC by 3.28--5.46 percentage points across eight matched parameter budgets. Paired reversals preserve the projection shapes and NSC scores yet worsen performance in both settings, exposing performance differences hidden by position-independent scoring. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/Optima-CityU/neural-spectral-capacity.

title: Loop to Look Better: Learning Adaptive Depth for Question-Guided Perception in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.

title: Bezier-Guided Adaptive Flow for Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by transferring useful preference knowledge across domains. However, users exhibit varying degrees of preference consistency across domains, while existing methods often rely on global alignment objectives or coarse-grained transfer strategies. Such approaches may introduce irrelevant information and provide limited flexibility in adapting semantic representations to individual user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose BGAFlow, a personalized framework that combines state-adaptive semantic evolution with user-specific transfer control. BGAFlow first establishes a shared semantic space through unified dual-domain pretraining with user profiles inferred by a large language model (LLM). Based on latent interest overlap, it then estimates a personalized horizon to determine the appropriate transfer extent for each user. To enable semantic adaptation, BGAFlow constructs a conditional Bezier curve as a geometric reference and learns a residual flow that progressively refines the trajectory based on intermediate preference states. The learned flow incorporates dynamic preference feedback to adjust transfer directions, while recommendation supervision and trajectory regularization encourage effective and smooth adaptation. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BGAFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the benefits of personalized transfer control and state-adaptive semantic evolution.

title: Nonlinear Drift Waves and Electrostatic Density Cavities in Upper Ionosphere
abstract: Nonlinear drift waves are investigated to explain the mechanism for the creation of one dimensional (1D) and two dimensional (2D) electrostatic density cavities in the presence of density gradient in direction perpendicular to the geomagnetic field. Ion motion along field lines has to be neglected for the formation of density depletion because nonlinear contribution of their parallel motion overcomes the effect of drift waves which create negative nonlinear potential. It is pointed out that a straightforward but appropriate model for drift waves can explain the generation of density cavities having widths in xy-plane if the external magnetic field is assumed to be along z-axis i.e. ${\bf B}_0 = B_0 \hat{z}$. The general nonlinear equation for drift waves takes the form of Zakharov-Kuznetson (ZK) equation when ion nonlinear vorticity term is ignored and it admits the solution in the form of 2D solitary wave. In 1D case, the ZK equation reduces to Korteweg de Vries (KdV) equation which admits solution in the form of 1D soliton. In both cases, the nonlinear potential becomes negative. The order of magnitude of the amplitude and width of density cavities is found to be in agreement with the satellite observations in upper ionosphere.

title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.

title: What Ethereum Developers Ask For, and Whether They Get It: Ten Years of Ethereum Stack Exchange
abstract: The Ethereum community learns where developers struggle through surveys and interviews, which record what developers say when asked about a chosen theme. Ethereum Stack Exchange (ESE) records what they ask for unprompted, and whether anyone resolves it. We study every question posted to ESE from Jan 2016 to Dec 2025, 54,637 in all, and label each with a prompt-based topic pipeline seeded with eight Ethereum-specific topics and open to new ones (22 topics in all). A three-provider committee of language models screens the labels, and manual adjudication of every disputed case puts their accuracy at 87.9 to 93.5%. Because the corpus is the complete record, no rate carries sampling error. We ask what developers ask for help with, whether the venue still resolves it, and, where it does not, whether the questions changed or their resolution did. Demand is concentrated on writing, deploying, and debugging contracts; the toolchain is the second-largest topic and growing, while security, consensus, and scaling are thin. Supply has weakened, and unevenly: answers still arrive, closure falls further. Across five estimators of the decade, the share of questions drawing any answer fell by 9.5 to 18.6 percentage points, but among answered questions the share reaching an accepted answer fell by 16.2 to 24.5. Rebuilding the later acceptance rate at the earlier topic mix moves the fall only from 9.40 to 9.32 points, so the topic mix does not explain it. Who asks separates outcomes far more sharply than what is asked: acceptance runs from 19.8% for askers below 10 reputation to 66.8% at 10k and above, a 47- point spread with a gradient in every year, against 17 across topics, and a shift toward newer askers accounts for up to 59% of the acceptance fall. The largest of seven properties an asker controls accompanies 5 points. The record places the support gap in the toolchain and among newcomers.

title: Arithmetic Conditions for the Invertibility of Circulant Matrices over Finite Fields
abstract: This paper investigates arithmetic conditions, over finite fields, for the invertibility of circulant matrices whose first row is $(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$, in terms of linear constraints on the entries $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$. The coefficients of such linear constraints are determined by field traces arising from Frobenius orbits of roots of unity, and under additional assumptions they are given by Ramanujan sums reduced modulo the characteristic of the given field. These results provide finite-field analogues of the corresponding criteria over $\mathbb{Q}$, where the relevant Ramanujan-sum linear constraints can be formulated without such additional assumptions, while also showing some differences caused by reduction modulo the characteristic. The constraints can often determine invertibility using aggregate information about the entries of a row, rather than the particular pattern of the entries. We also discuss the polynomial gcd criterion, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for invertibility and yields further consequences for special families of circulant matrices.

title: Surface morphology and shear effect on lubricated granular system
abstract: Improving the particle surface frictional behavior is of considerable importance in several industries so as to manipulate the powder flowability and handling. In this work, we have studied the lubrication phenomena in an assembly of flowing bulk powder particles in presence of a fine powder lubricant. Experiments were conducted in two different shear environments, for two different levels of confinement and using three different bulk powder particles having distinct surface morphology. The added lubricant particles tend to adhere to the surface of bulk particles thereby altering their surface morphology. This results in altered inter-particle friction, which typically reduces for small addition of lubricant, but increases on its excess addition, thereby altering the particle flowability. While this behavior is generally understood through previous studies, the current work explores how the effect of confinement, shear environment and particle surface characteristics combine in a unique manner to provide modified flow behavior for different lubricant concentrations. Extended shear duration seems to extend the range of lubricant concentrations for improved flowability. On the other hand flow confinement seems to limit the extent of lubrication for these range of concentrations. Both these opposing effects also exhibit a unique dependence on the particle surface morphology and its seeming affinity with the lubricant particle. The parameter types and ranges explored comprise most conditions encountered in industrial systems, the outcome thereby providing a basis for designing of applications handling lubricant-particle mixtures.

title: Radial Schur multipliers on trees and quantitative Fourier--Schur separation
abstract: We study ordinary and completely bounded norms of radial Schur multipliers on trees. On the homogeneous tree of countably infinite degree, we show that boundedness implies complete boundedness. The argument realizes arbitrary matrix amplifications of a shifted Toeplitz symbol inside rectangular corners of the original multiplier. It also applies to some locally finite trees of unbounded degree. Consequently, the completely bounded radial multiplier theorem of González-Pérez, Parcet, Pérez García and Wang has no general counterpart with ordinary norms. We also determine the optimal order of the comparison constant for positive definite even symbols. For each $1 < p < \infty$ with $p \neq 2$, we construct radial symbols on finitely generated nonabelian free groups, supported in the ball of radius $N$, whose completely bounded Herz--Schur norms remain bounded as $N \to \infty$, whereas their ordinary Fourier multiplier norms grow at least like $N^{|1-\frac{2}{p}|}$. For each fixed $0 < \vartheta < π$, we also determine the exact order $t^{-|1-\frac{2}{p}|}$ of both the ordinary and completely bounded Fourier multiplier norms of the damped radial phases $s \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{(-t+\mathrm{i}\vartheta)|s|}$ as $t \to 0$. Finally, we compute the local amenability modulus of free balls, we bound the Fourier--Schur ratio of free balls from above and below in terms of this modulus, and we show that its restriction to radial symbols grows polynomially in the radius.

title: Light pulse propagation through a dielectric slab. II. Two roads to the same field: numerical cross-validation of local (FDTD-ADE) and non-local (retarded integral-equation) solutions
abstract: Paper I of this series (arXiv:2610.29336) solves, via the retarded Green's functions, the local differential equations governing light propagation in a plane-parallel dielectric slab, obtaining a pair of retarded integral equations that represent, at the continuum level, the microscopic multiple-scattering picture underlying the local formulation. The two formulations are thus proven to be analytically equivalent. The local system of differential equations is then solved numerically with a finite-difference time-domain scheme (FDTD-ADE). This report closes the loop by solving the retarded integral equations directly, without passing through the local formulation, and comparing the result with the FDTD-ADE solution under the same physical and material conditions. The two independently implemented, structurally different numerical schemes agree within 0.02-1.3% for the reported reflected and transmitted energy fractions; the absorbed fraction, computed independently in both schemes from the Lorentz damping term rather than merely inferred from 1-R-T, agrees closely between the two methods, to the precision reported. Both solutions are also compared with an exact reference, the Airy formula weighted over the pulse spectrum: the direct solution reproduces it to within 0.3%, and its Richardson extrapolation to all digits shown. The agreement persists for a few-cycle pulse and for a sub-wavelength slab, where naive fixed-point iteration of the integral equations is not a practical convergent strategy. A complementary set of movie-style, nine-frame visualizations is also presented, illustrating the same equivalence directly in the field rather than only in integrated observables. To the author's knowledge, a direct numerical cross-validation of these two formulations in this genuinely time-dependent regime has not previously been reported.

title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.

title: Central limit theorem for the Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation
abstract: We establish the central limit theorem (CLT) for Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation of Langevin equations with state-dependent, possibly non-symmetric friction and multiplicative noise. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such result, even in the case of constant friction and additive noise. The result differs in an essential way from classical averaging CLTs and reveals a new two-scale fluctuation phenomenon. The normalized difference process retains a persistent fast component and is generally not tight in $C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$, thus the usual continuous-path CLT cannot hold. We derive an exact decomposition of the normalized difference into an accumulated slow fluctuation and a rapidly relaxing velocity correction. The auxiliary slow fluctuation converges to a linear diffusion driven by both the original Brownian motion and an additional independent Brownian noise whose effective covariance is characterized explicitly through a quadratic Poisson corrector. For every fixed $t>0$, the fast correction converges conditionally to its local Gaussian equilibrium. Consequently, the fixed-time fluctuation limit is identified as a Gaussian mixture: $$ \frac{\bar X_t-X_t^\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}} \Longrightarrow \bar Y_t+N^{1/2}(\bar X_t)ξ, $$ where $\bar X_t$ is the overdamped limit, $\bar Y_t$ is the limiting slow fluctuation, $N$ is the covariance of the terminal velocity correction and solves a Lyapunov equation, and $ξ$ is a standard Gaussian random variable independent of $(\bar X_t,\bar Y_t)$. A quantitative convergence rate is also provided. The result fills the remaining gap in the asymptotic theory of the overdamped approximation at the central limit scale, complementing the existing law of large numbers, moderate deviation and large deviation results.

title: Exceptional point structure and chiral state transfer in a rate-operator-engineered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Bose-Hubbard dimer
abstract: The rate operator quantum jumps (ROQJ) is a general method to unravel a master equation describing the dynamics of an open quantum system into stochastic pure state trajectories. By post-selecting on no jumps occurring, one obtains a trajectory generated by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The ROQJ allows for versatile modification of this non-Hermitian evolution, with each non-Hermitian Hamiltonian corresponding to a different continuous measurement scheme. We apply the ROQJ to modify the non-Hermitian dynamics of the open three-particle Bose-Hubbard dimer model under environmental non-local dephasing to construct a $PT$-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with a general two parameter $PT$-symmetric imaginary diagonal part, which generalizes the well-known gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. We characterize the symmetry structure of the spectrum for different on-site interaction strengths. For vanishing on-site interaction, we find the unbroken $PT$-symmetry region enclosed by order two exceptional lines of different character and four order four exceptional points, two of which are not found in the usual gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. Additionally, we find regions with degenerate imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, also not found in the gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. In this parameter space, we use time-dependent rate operator transformations to investigate state transfer under slowly varying parameter loops. Loops encircling an order four exceptional point exhibit chiral state transfer. Because the loops cross exceptional lines, the final states are superpositions of eigenstates. Chiral state transfer is also found with non-zero homogeneous on-site interaction when the loop crosses over broken $PT$-symmetry regions of different character. Using inhomogeneous on-site interactions, we find direction dependent state transfer between eigenstates without crossing or encircling exceptional points.

title: A homological approach to Dax invariants
abstract: We present a homological construction of Dax invariants in 4-manifolds that is intrinsic to the topological category and requires neither smoothing nor generic representatives. Applications include an extension of the invariant of Cha-Kim to neat disks without assuming local flatness, and a topological definition of the Dax map for arc spaces that yields a short alternative proof of the topological Dax isomorphism theorem.

title: Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks: Enhancing Flexibility in Node Dependencies via penalized B-Splines
abstract: Bayesian networks for continuous variables often rely on restrictive assumptions: linear Gaussian models lack flexibility to capture nonlinear dependencies, while non-parametric approaches provide greater flexibility at a high computational cost. This creates a gap for modeling scenarios where variables are approximately Gaussian but exhibit nonlinear relationships. We introduce Semi-Linear Gaussian Bayesian Networks (SLGBN), a novel class of continuous Bayesian networks designed to bridge this gap, preserving Gaussian conditional distributions while introducing nonlinear conditional mean functions. The proposed framework provides a unified probabilistic framework combining linear Gaussian and nonlinear Gaussian conditional models within the same Bayesian network Nonlinear conditional mean functions are estimated using generalized additive models (GAMs) with penalized B-splines. We present parameter estimation procedures for both types of nodes, as well as a greedy hill-climbing algorithm for learning the network structure under the SLGBN framework. To assess its performance, we compare SLGBN with other continuous Bayesian network models, including semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBN) and Linear Gaussian Bayesian networks (LGBN). Experimental results evaluate both goodness of fit and the ability to recover the underlying network structure. The results show that, in the presence of nonlinear Gaussian relationships, SLGBN achieves better fit and improved structure recovery compared to alternative models, particularly when combined with the Extended Bayesian Information Criterion (EBIC*) score. Furthermore, by retaining Gaussian conditional distributions, SLGBN offers computational advantages over fully semiparametric approaches.

title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.

title: Discovering supernovae in the Virgo Cluster during the LSST era
abstract: In the era of unprecedentedly wide, deep and high-cadence sky surveys the chance for discovering new explosive transients in nearby, rich galaxy clusters within hours after explosion is expected to increase dramatically. In this paper we focus on the Virgo cluster ($D \simeq 16.5$ Mpc), and estimate the expected numbers of new, very young supernovae in different sub-structures and galaxy types of the cluster during the proposed lifetime (~10 years) of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) by the Vera Rubin Observatory. These predictions will be tested observationally during the ongoing Shadow-LSST discovery and follow-up program led by University of Arizona in the upcoming years.

title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.

title: A neural-network model to find correlations in astrochemical space
abstract: The detection of new interstellar molecules is central to astrochemistry, and arguably the most transformative development in the field in past decade has been the increase in both number and diversity of detected species. Using natural language processing models, we develop a machine-learning pipeline, similar to other approaches reported in the literature, to connect molecular structures, encoded as chemical strings, and molecular column densities in TMC-1. The workflow generates astrochemically informed embeddings that can be employed in subsequent supervised learning tasks. These representations are used within a neural-network framework to perform column-density regression on both the original molecular inventory and out-of-distribution species. The resulting model achieves mean squared error values of 0.17/0.58 and mean absolute error values of 0.29/0.59, and coefficients of determination of 0.88/0.51 for the train+validation and validation datasets. The latent vectors learned by the model are rich mathematical objects that capture the underlying chemical relations and also the potential interstellar detectability of the molecule. Using these vectors in molecules obtained from systematic permutations of the TMC-1 inventory, we identify several promising candidates for future detection in this cloud, together with a large number of apolar species. By training the model on datasets reflecting different historical epochs of molecular detections in TMC-1, we show that recent molecular detections have substantially reshaped our understanding of interstellar chemistry, in a transformative, rather than incremental, way. Beyond accurate prediction of column-density trends for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution molecules, the latent-space representations produced by the model provide a stepping stone for developing new forms of data-driven astrochemical intuition and exploration.

title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
abstract: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of real-world short queries paired with ground-truth Mathlib statements makes this ambiguity even more intractable. We argue that this is essentially a data problem. Through adversarial training, we scale up the generation of labeled short and ambiguous queries, and learn to disambiguate user queries at both model-level fine-tuning and input-level query rewriting. On the human-curated MathlibQR benchmark, our Lean Finder V2 sets a new state of the art, with at least 11% relative improvement over the previous best Mathlib semantic search engines. On top of our state-of-the-art retriever, optimized query rewriting further improves MathlibQR retrieval. On unlabeled queries from human and coding-agent interactions, Lean Finder V2 is ranked as the strongest system. Integrated with Claude Code, Lean Finder V2 improves proof success on downstream theorem-proving task. Lean Finder V2 is available at: https://leanfinder.github.io/

title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
abstract: Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher's full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions. We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student-generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter. In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher-generated action. The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher's preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees.

title: Bipartite solutions of the set-theoretic Yang--Baxer equation
abstract: We introduce a new class of unitary set-theoretic Yang--Baxter solutions, called \emph{bipartite} solutions. This class, which is purely combinatorial in nature, forms a full subcategory of $\mathcal{LYB}$, the category of Lyubashenko type solutions of Agore, Chirvasitu and the author, and is particularly amenable to explicit classification results. We give an intrinsic necessary and sufficient condition for a solution of the Yang--Baxter equation to be isomorphic to a bipartite solution, we settle the isomorphism problem within this class and, as an application, we determine their automorphism groups. If $X$ is a finite set with $|X| = n$, the number of isomorphism classes of bipartite solutions on $X$ is $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1 + \sum_{m=2}^{n} \bigl( o(m, n-m) - 1 \bigr)$, where $o(m, k)$ denotes the number of orbits of the symmetric group $S_m$ acting by conjugation on the $k$-element multisets of elements of $S_m$. The paper also offers a comparative study: for small $|X| = n$ we count, up to isomorphism, all set-theoretic Yang--Baxter solutions on $X$, together with five distinguished families of solutions. Throughout the range we were able to compute, the class $\mathcal{LYB}$ accounts for a large share of all bijective and of all non-degenerate solutions, strikingly close to the total.

title: Fit-error corrected auxiliary master equation approach for low-temperature nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory
abstract: The auxiliary master equation approach (AMEA) is a nonperturbative impurity solver for steady-state nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). It replaces the physical hybridization function by that of a small auxiliary open quantum system, whose parameters are fitted to reproduce it, and then solves the resulting many-body problem essentially exactly. AMEA's accuracy is thus limited by the quality of this fit: since the fastest-varying part of the hybridization is set by the distribution function, whose Fermi edges sharpen at low temperature, the fit tends to overestimate the temperature, especially for weak reservoir coupling. For the auxiliary hybridization itself, however, AMEA's self-energy is essentially exact. We correct for the fit error by estimating, via an approximate solver applicable to arbitrary hybridization functions, the ratio between the self-energies of the physical and auxiliary hybridizations, and using it to extend AMEA's self-energy from the auxiliary to the physical case. This fit-error correction becomes exact whenever either the fit or the approximate solver is exact. We benchmark the scheme using the nonequilibrium Kajueter-Kotliar iterated perturbation theory (IPT), generalized here to spin-polarized solutions, as the approximate solver; other approximate solvers, such as the noncrossing approximation, can be used as well. Applied to an Anderson impurity model with a spin-polarized bath, and within DMFT to a Hubbard layer weakly coupled to two metallic reservoirs, the correction largely removes the spurious heating from the AMEA fit and from insufficient thermalization by the reservoirs, while preserving the correct description of the Mott insulator, which IPT alone cannot fully recover.

title: Bifurcations from Weight Space: JEPAWG on Parametric Dynamical Systems
abstract: Trained network weights are increasingly treated as data, but there is rarely ground truth about what a population of models should encode, which hampers systematic validation of weight-space methods. This makes parametric dynamical systems a natural test-bed: the dynamics change qualitatively at submanifolds of parameter space that are, in well-studied families, known analytically or numerically. Fine-tuning a forecasting network at each point of a parameter grid yields a model zoo indexed by a physical parameter, against which weight-space diagnostics can be checked. We build such model zoos for four dynamical systems and analyse them with JEPAWG, a recently proposed joint-embedding hypernetwork built around a learned parameter--weight representation. It was first introduced for neural samplers for lattice field theories, where its latent geometry located the phase transition and estimated the 2D Ising critical exponent. Applied to dynamical systems, JEPAWG is competitive on forecasting with a hypernetwork trained directly for that task, despite being supervised on the parameter--weight correspondence rather than on forecasts. Beyond forecasting, the norm of the parameter-derivative of the decoded weights locates Hopf points and curves, tracks a period-doubling cascade closely enough to give a qualitative estimate of the Feigenbaum constant, and detects a global bifurcation, which has no eigenvalue signature and is therefore invisible to linearisation. As such, JEPAWG provides interpretable insight into the dynamics that is not available from other hypernetworks. Together, these results indicate that JEPAWG is a workable instrument for reading physical structure off a population of trained networks.

title: Locally symmetric hypersurfaces in globally symmetric spaces
abstract: We classify locally symmetric hypersurfaces, understood in the intrinsic sense, in Riemannian globally symmetric spaces.

title: Surface Defects in the $\mathcal{N}=2$ Lens Space Index and Elliptic Integrability
abstract: We determine the surface-defect difference operators of the 4d $\mathcal{N}=2$ lens space index for class $\mathcal{S}$ theories of type $A_{N-1}$ on $(\mathbb{S}^3/\mathbb{Z}_r)\times\mathbb{S}^1$. For generic fugacities $(p,q,t)$ and arbitrary rank $N$, orbifold order $r$ and discrete holonomies, their coefficients are finite products of theta functions with nomes $p^r$ and $q^r$. After an explicit gauge transformation, Gaussian in the holonomies, each operator factorizes into two elliptic Ruijsenaars--Schneider-type operators with step $pq$, one with nome $p^r$ and one with nome $q^r$, acting on variables glued along a lattice. Using this factorization and a Wronski-type relation, we prove that all the operators commute. We also establish a sufficient criterion for self-adjointness with respect to the bilinear vector multiplet pairing. It applies to the basic mixed operator and, in suitable parameter chambers, to the pure $p$- and $q$-type operators; for general mixed operators the contour prescription remains open. These results support the expectations from S-duality.

title: Spontaneous chiral-symmetry breaking in four-dimensional QCD with $A_x=A_y=0$ projection in dimensional reduction gauge
abstract: We investigate spontaneous chiral-symmetry breaking in four-dimensional (4D) QCD in the dimensional reduction (DR) gauge, defined so as to minimize $R_{\mathrm{DR}}\equiv~\int d^{4}s ~ \mathrm{Tr} \left[ A_{x}^{2}(s) + A_{y}^{2}(s) \right]$. We consider ``$tz$-projection" of $A_{x,y}(s) \to 0$ and ``$xy$-projection" of $A_{t,z}(s) \to 0$, respectively, for the gauge configuration generated in the DR gauge, in a similar sense to Abelian, monopole and photon projections in the maximally Abelian gauge. The chiral condensate is estimated from the low-lying Dirac-eigenvalue density $ρ(λ)$ using the Banks-Casher relation. By the $tz$-projection in the DR gauge, the chiral condensate is largely reserved. In contrast, the chiral condensate becomes zero by the $xy$-projection in the DR gauge. This indicates that $A_{t}(s)$ and $A_{z}(s)$ play a dominant role, while $A_{x}(s)$ and $A_{y}(s)$ play no role, in spontaneous chiral-symmetry breaking in the DR gauge.

title: ADAPT for Science: A Multi-Agent System for Self-Evolving Scientific Optimization
abstract: Scientific discovery often requires identifying a small number of high-performing designs in vast, constrained search spaces. This is difficult when evaluations are costly, feasible solutions are sparse, parameters are strongly coupled, and physical constraints are strict. Recent AI for AI methods can automatically improve algorithms and optimization procedures. However, general purpose approaches are not designed around scientific priors, physical constraints, and limited evaluation budgets. We introduce ADAPT for Science, a multi-agent framework that treats scientific optimization as two coupled decisions: where to search and how to search. ADAPT uses historical designs to identify promising and diverse initial conditions, progressively concentrates computation on favorable search directions, and evolves the optimization procedure from execution feedback. We evaluate ADAPT on the design of gravitational wave detectors using a differentiable physics simulator and eight unseen detector topologies. Under matched scientific evaluation budgets, ADAPT achieves a mean loss of 0.204 +/- 0.101, reducing loss by 54.9% relative to the best classical optimizer and by 62.2% relative to the best general purpose agentic evolution baseline. ADAPT achieves the lowest loss on all unseen topologies among the evaluated baselines. ADAPT provides a step toward scientific optimization systems that continuously learn from prior experience and their own search outcomes.

title: Stiff source terms inside ADER-DG method
abstract: ADER-DG numerical method with the LST-DG predictor, when used to solve hyperbolic equations with stiff source terms, exhibits properties characteristic of IMEX computational schemes. With increasing stiffness, characterized by the parameter $z = ν{Δt}^{n} < 0$, the maximum of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}$ of the ADER-DG numerical method increases. In the region of strong stiffness $|z| \gg 1$, a linear increase in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z) \sim |z|$ occurs. In the region of small source terms $|z| \ll 1$, the results $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ transform into known results for the problem $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(0)$ without source terms. In the transition region $|z| \sim 1$, a range of insignificant decrease in the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(z)$ is discovered. In the linear case, instability is violated precisely when one of the matrix eigenvalues reaches $λ= -1$, regardless of the phase $θ$ of the numerical solution. A rigorous stability theory of the ADER-DG numerical method for stiff problems for arbitrary degree $N$ of basis polynomials is constructed. The stability condition is simplified to solving a polynomial equation for the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}$. Highly accurate dependencies of the Courant number $\mathrm{CFL}_{\rm max}(N, z)$ of the ADER-DG method on the parameter $z$ are obtained. A rigorous direct proof of the approximation of the ADER-DG method is presented. Approximation orders $p = N+1$ for arbitrary degrees $N$ are rigorously derived. A set of numerical experiments is carried out to apply the ADER-DG method to solving both a linear advection-reaction equation and the system of Euler equations for a two-component reacting medium. The results obtained in these calculations confirm the theoretical results well.

title: Training Mixed-Monotone Neural Networks for Verification Without Set Propagation
abstract: Most formal verification approaches for neural networks conservatively enclose the output set of the neural network. However, computing a tight output enclosure is in general computationally hard. We sidestep this challenge with a novel neural network architecture that realizes mixed-monotone functions as the difference of monotone subnetworks. By utilizing the theory on mixed-monotone systems, this reduces the computation of a tight output enclosure from complicated set propagation to two simple forward passes of opposite corners of an input interval. Moreover, because the size of the resulting enclosure is a closed-form function of the weights of the neural network, we can directly minimize it during training. We prove a lower bound on the size of any such enclosure, given by the total variation of the represented function generalized to several inputs, which makes it possible to compare the tightness of the enclosure against the optimum. Our evaluation on regression and dynamical-system benchmarks demonstrates that our training reduces the enclosure size to within 0.5% of the lower bound without sacrificing prediction accuracy. Computing our enclosure is orders of magnitude faster than CROWN and $α$-CROWN and on deep networks it is also tighter than zonotope propagation and CROWN, while its size exceeds that of $α$-CROWN by only 5.1%.

title: CAVC: Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache for Modality-Asymmetric Diffusion Generation
abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.

title: From Turing Patterns to Spike Self-Replication and Nucleation in a Growing-Domain Tulip Breaking Virus Model
abstract: A recently proposed reaction-diffusion model for the tulip breaking virus (TBV) has been shown to generate striped pigmentation patterns on growing tulip petals. In this paper, we investigate the formation of localized spike patterns in this model in the asymptotic limit of small viral diffusivity. It is known that two distinct bifurcation mechanisms can occur which generate new spikes as the domain half-length $L$ slowly increases: spike self-replication and spike nucleation. Self-replication occurs through a saddle-node bifurcation of the inner spike core problem, whereas nucleation is associated with a fold of the nonlinear outer problem. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive critical conditions for these mechanisms and construct phase diagrams that predict which mechanism occurs first as $L$ increases, or whether nucleation is absent. We further combine these results with a Turing instability analysis of the homogeneous steady state to obtain a phase diagram of pattern-forming mechanisms. An interesting finding is that, for the TBV model, the Turing-unstable region lies entirely within the parameter regime where spike nucleation is possible. These results provide further insight into the mechanisms underlying the formation and evolution of pigmentation patterns in virus-infected tulips.

title: System-Level Evaluation of Uplink Access Schemes for Ambient IoT
abstract: Ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT) devices operate under stringent energy constraints, relying on harvested power in the $μ$W-to-mW range and limited energy storage. The A-IoT air interface for active devices is still under development; we therefore use Narrowband Internet of Things (NB-IoT) as an implementable reference for evaluating autonomous Uplink (UL) access under harvested energy. Under these conditions, the standard NB-IoT contention-based Random Access (RA) procedure incurs substantial per-packet overhead, making UL access in dense A-IoT networks increasingly energy-expensive. Context-retaining UL access schemes reduce this overhead, but their energy-latency trade-offs are insufficiently studied in literature under realistic harvesting and protocol constraints. To address this gap, we extend the LENA-NB ns-3 module with solar energy harvesting, supercapacitor storage, and a hysteretic brown-out mechanism, and propose Hybrid Scheduling Request (HSR), a hybrid UL access scheme combining reserved request occasions with opportunistic contention. We compare RA, Scheduling Request (SR), HSR and an Idealized Fast Uplink Grant (FUG) serving as a performance bound. Results show that HSR reduces mean packet delay by up to 69% and SR reduces energy per delivered bit by up to 24%, both relative to RA.

title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures
abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2π=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.

title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
abstract: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.

title: The signless Laplacian spectral Turán problems for disjoint triangles
abstract: The classical Turán-type problem for graphs forbidding $k$ disjoint triangles has been resolved firstly by Erdős [Arch. Math. 13 (1962) 222-227] for graphs of sufficiently large order and improved by Moon [Canad. J. Math. 20 (1968) 95-102], who established that the unique edge extremal graph is $K_{k-1}\vee T_2(n-k+1)$ for $n> \frac{19k-11}{2}$. In this paper, we determine the maximum signless Laplacian spectral radius among all $kK_3$-free graphs of order $n$ and characterize the unique signless Laplacian spectral extremal graph $K_{k-1}\vee T_{2}(n-k+1)$ for all $k\ge 2$ and sufficiently large $n$.

title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark
abstract: Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.

title: Direct Forcing: A Single-Stage Training Recipe for Few-Step Autoregressive Text-to-Video Generation
abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.

title: Inverse KLT kernel of AdS string-amplitude building blocks from the intersection matrix
abstract: We develop a topological and combinatorial interpretation of the Kawai--Lewellen--Tye (KLT) relations for $n$-point AdS string-amplitude building blocks, which are disk integrals with multivariable multiple polylogarithm insertions and sphere integrals with their single-valued counterparts. Building on the framework of twisted de Rham theory over a noncommutative ring, we reformulate the problem in terms of associahedral chambers of the moduli space loaded with solutions of the Knizhnik--Zamolodchikov equation.
