To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

title: Gamma conjectures for Milnor hypersurfaces
abstract: We prove Gamma conjectures I and II of Galkin, Golyshev and Iritani for Milnor hypersurfaces, the smooth hypersurfaces of bidegree $(1,1)$ in the product of two projective spaces. We provide a criterion for Gamma conjecture II for general Fano manifolds, generalizing the criterion by Hu and Ke. Using the mirror symmetry technique of Galkin and Iritani, we establish global Gamma-I for Milnor hypersurfaces, thereby proving Gamma conjecture I as a special case. Using it, together with the Galois action and our criterion, we verify Gamma conjecture II for Milnor hypersurfaces.

title: Influence of nanoparticle shapes in nanofluid film boiling on vertical cylinders: A numerical study
abstract: This research explores how nanoparticle shapes affect the thermal behavior of nanofluid film boiling along a vertical cylinder, using a Continuous-Species-Transfer method within a Computational Multi-Fluid Dynamics framework. The behavior of nanoparticles in both liquid and vapor phases is modeled, accounting for Brownian motion and thermophoresis. A comprehensive two-dimensional axisymmetric analysis is conducted to investigate the effects of various Al2O3 nanoparticle shapes, including spheres, bricks, blades, cylinders, and platelets, on boiling heat transfer. The results demonstrate that nanoparticle shape has a minimal impact on deposition dynamics but significantly affects kinematic viscosity, particularly for platelet-shaped nanoparticles. Blade-shaped nanoparticles provide substantial enhancement of thermal transport, as indicated by pronounced temperature gradients and increased thermal conductivity. These nanoparticles also improve the Nusselt number, suggesting enhanced boiling heat transfer efficiency. This improvement is particularly significant at higher nanoparticle concentrations, although the relationship is not strictly linear. Future work will explore different nanoparticle materials, boiling scenarios, and experimental validation.

title: WildFakeToolBench: Benchmarking AI-Generated Image Detectors with Web-Sourced Image Processing
abstract: As AI generated images are getting popular these days, discussions on such generations are widely existed in current public forums, software repositories, and photography tutorials. Moreover, with the help of LLM-assisted code translation, malicious actors can adopt such information to evade detectors without specialized knowledge or local GPU execution of the resulting tools. To evaluate such risks, we introduce \textsc{WildFakeToolBench}, a benchmark suite of $156$ executable image-processing tools derived from $220$ public sources across $142$ domains. Each tool retains its source evidence and passes syntax, execution, and output-distortion checks without using feedback from the evaluated detectors. On $105$ generated images from five generators, we evaluate six state-of-the-art detectors with images processed by the tools in our collected bench to assess their effectiveness against such in-the-wild risks. The strongest individual tools achieve attack success rates of $25.25\%$--$100\%$ across detectors, exceeding the strongest of six selected image-processing baselines for each detector. Evaluating subsets of an eight-tool pool yields worst-case coverage above $80\%$ for every detector. Effectiveness is sparse and detector-specific: high coverage across candidates does not imply reliable one-shot evasion. These findings not only highlight the potential of such web-sourced risks, but also show the potential on establishing AI-image detector robustness evaluation framework based on those in-the-wild information.

title: Balanced Posted Prices in Stationary Two-Sided Markets
abstract: We study an intermediary that buys nonperishing items from arriving sellers and sells them to arriving buyers, subject to limited storage. Sellers and buyers arrive according to independent Poisson processes. The intermediary pays and charges the same fixed item prices, aiming to maximize long-run gains from trade: buyer value minus seller cost. Our benchmark may choose allocations directly, has unlimited storage, and must purchase each unit before allocating it. Its optimal long-run gain rate equals the value of a linear program of average purchase and allocation rates, with or without knowledge of future arrivals. For buyers whose bundle values are maxima of nonnegative additive valuations (XOS), we compute static common prices that guarantee half of this benchmark for arbitrary finite item capacities, even one storage slot per item, regardless of how ties are resolved without using future arrivals. The prices are computable in polynomial time using demand and supporting-value queries. The construction equalizes itemwise lower bounds on buyer and seller contributions to gains from trade, accounting for procurement costs. We call this contribution balance. As a single-item foundation, we also equalize the rates of purchases and sales selected by the price, before checking inventory availability. We call this rate balance. For capacity $C$, it yields the tight guarantee $C/(C+1)$. The two principles parallel proofs of the classical prophet inequality based on half the expected benchmark and on a median threshold, adapting these balancing ideas to recurring two-sided markets with limited inventory.

title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities
abstract: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and able to resist perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Theoretical approaches to this problem typically require making strict assumptions about the structure, parameters and functional forms used in models, hindering general insight. Here, we address this problem by developing and analyzing a generalized model of microbial community dynamics, capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach allows us to assess the stability of microbial systems across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure and non-linear dynamics. Our analysis shows how community stability is constrained by system size and identifies its key metabolic and dynamical drivers, highlighting the central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity. Furthermore, we show how the structure of communities mediates their stability, allowing communities to counteract the destabilizing cross-feeding loops through organization into hierarchical trophic structures. Together, these results provide new insight into the stability of microbial communities and offer a flexible analytical framework for future work to explore the responses of communities to perturbation.

title: Self-averaging enables reconstruction of higher-order chaotic networks
abstract: Higher-order interactions create a combinatorial space of candidate dynamical terms, making network reconstruction difficult when node dynamics, coupling functions and interaction topology are unknown. Here we identify a regime in which weakly coupled higher-order chaotic networks admit a higher-order interaction reduction. Weak coupling largely preserves the statistical structure of intrinsic chaotic motion, while dense higher-order neighborhoods provide repeated sampling of weakly correlated multi-node inputs received by hub nodes. Consequently, the aggregate interaction field can be represented by a compact function of the hub state, together with a node-dependent offset and finite-neighborhood fluctuations. We exploit this reduction to learn dynamically relevant coupling forms and reconstruct interactions of different orders by sparse regression. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the framework within an effective region of the tested coupling-parameter space, including representative weak-coupling settings. Reconstruction remains stable at the larger network sizes and higher hub-neighborhood densities examined. Additional tests on networks constructed from empirical topologies show that structural priors reduce data requirements and that the framework remains applicable to heterogeneous chaotic dynamics. These results identify reduction of aggregate higher-order inputs as an interpretable route to dimensional compression and joint dynamical and structural reconstruction.

title: Calibration-free IMU-based Relative Orientation Estimation under Dynamic Human Motion
abstract: Recent magnetometer-free inertial measurement unit (IMU) methods can reduce drift in joint motion estimation using rigid-body constraints, but they typically require pre-calibrated sensor locations, assumptions of specific joint models (e.g., hinge joints) or limited motion types, or an external reference for global orientation. Furthermore, challenges related to high-frequency impacts (e.g. at foot strikes during gait) and numerical differentiation of noisy measurements have not been explicitly addressed. We propose an extended Kalman filter that estimates relative IMU orientation and sensor location simultaneously, requiring neither offline sensor location calibration nor a global orientation anchor. A systematic simulation study shows that the quality of the relative orientation and the sensor location estimates depends on different motion-intensity sources: the joint center acceleration and the relative angular velocity, respectively. A low-pass filter (LPF) is used to mitigate real-signal outliers before applying the rigid-body constraint. When applied to the OpenSense dataset with real IMU measurements across four subjects with three lower-body joint types during walking and complex tasks including various motion types, the proposed method achieves an overall relative orientation error of 2.61°, compared with 10.40° for a baseline using offline-estimated sensor locations and 7.43° for a baseline using marker-derived sensor locations. These results show that the proposed calibration-free estimation framework handles real IMU data effectively and achieves accurate relative orientation without offline sensor location calibration.

title: Functional understanding of structural components in polypseudorotaxane gels
abstract: Biomedical devices, wearable interfaces, and soft robots require compliant soft materials with reliable mechanical performance, yet the molecular principles needed to design such materials are not always fully understood. Thus, there is an urgent need to understand how to design novel stretchable and soft hydrogels with enhanced toughness, i.e. resistance to breakage. Slide-ring gels (SRGs) are a class of unconventional soft materials formed by polyrotaxanes (PR) building blocks whereby sliding cyclodextrins (CD) replace traditional chemical and physical crosslinks and in turn enhance toughness and stretchability by several orders of magnitude. The rational design of SRGs re- mains challenging due to a lack of a mechanistic understanding of the role played by individual components. In this work, we implement simple synthetic perturbations that individually target polymer-CD and CD-CD interactions in unstoppered pseudopolyrotaxanes (pPR) solutions and measure the consequent changes in viscoelastic properties. Weakening the intermolecular interaction between CDs abolishes crystallisation and significantly weakens the gel. At the same time, thermodynamically favouring threading by using azobenzene-modified PEG chains favours the formation of stable and long-lived networks even at remarkably low CD stoichiometries. We rationalise these observations with coarse-grained Molecular Dynamics simulations which clarify the structure-function relationship of the components forming these materials. Our work contributes to guiding the rational design and development of enhanced SRG hydrogels and elastomers.

title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.

title: Beyond city pairs: Higher-order information in urban growth across borders
abstract: We apply higher-order information measures to urban growth across borders and spatial units. We analyse 8,808 functional urban areas using gridded GDP estimates allocated from national accounts. Negative estimated O-information occurs in 29.93% of cross-border triplets and 2.00% of domestic triplets. This fifteen-fold contrast falls to fourfold at comparable dependence strength and persists under data-quality restrictions. Target-specific decompositions show how information overlaps or combines across cities. Administrative subdivisions have mean O-information within matched random-map ranges inside countries. These findings show why interpreting geographic dependence requires specifying comparison cities and spatial units, while economic connections remain to be established independently.

title: Towards Field-Deployable Wearable IMU Systems for Occupational Activity Recognition
abstract: Wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) systems for construction worker human activity recognition (HAR) routinely report aggregate accuracies above 95 %, rarely under genuine subject-independent (leave-one-subject-out (LOSO)) evaluation, masking the per-individual variance that determines real-world deployment performance. Using the VTT-ConIoT benchmark, we conduct, to our knowledge, the first systematic configuration sensitivity analysis of this dataset: six classifiers across five sensor placements and three window sizes under a single LOSO protocol, a personalised-calibration pilot, and a validated comparison of tabular GAN-based and standard time-series augmentation. Per-subject LOSO accuracy for the main multi-sensor, 16-class configuration ranges from 61.9 % to 88.7 % (mean 77.5 %), a 27 pp spread, though all data are laboratory-collected. Multi-sensor fusion and longer windows both improve accuracy; standard augmentation gives small, consistent gains, while Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) augmentation actively harms accuracy with a demonstrated distributional-fidelity mechanism; and personalised calibration recovers 16.8 pp for the weakest participants from just 30 % of their own data. These findings provide evidence-grounded configuration guidance for scaling occupational body sensor networks towards field deployment

title: Accurate ab initio calculations of the ground state properties of singly charged alkali metal hydrides
abstract: In this article, we investigate the ground state electronic properties of singly charged alkali metal hydrides using the single-reference coupled-cluster method with single and double excitations (CCSD), together with perturbative triple excitations (CCSD(T)). A large relativistic core-valence quintuple-zeta basis set has been employed. The calculated spectroscopic constants and molecular properties are compared with existing data in the literature. Further, the relevant vibrational parameters are determined by solving the vibrational Schrödinger equation utilizing potential energy curves and permanent dipole moment curves. Thereafter, spontaneous and black-body radiation induced transition rates are calculated to obtain the lifetimes of the vibrational states.

title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
abstract: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.

title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
abstract: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.

title: A local-to-global principle for $f$-divergence homogenization
abstract: We study the effect of replacing a family of independent statistical experiments by independent repetitions of their average. We give a simple, complete characterization of the $f$-divergences for which this operation increases divergence by at most a constant depending only on the generator, uniformly in the number of observations and the underlying measurable space. The characterization is governed by a local-to-global principle: a comparison restricted to two observations on a binary alphabet already determines the validity of the general inequality. It admits an explicit scalar formulation, which simplifies further for symmetric divergences. The result applies to arbitrary convex generators and requires no differentiability or symmetry assumptions. It recovers the homogenization inequality for total variation and identifies exactly the admissible members of the power-divergence family. In particular, whenever uniform homogenization fails, the obstruction is already present in a family of binary experiments with two observations. Moreover, the global comparison constant is controlled uniformly over generators with a common bound in the local inequality.

title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).

title: Liouville Theorems and Sharp Homogeneity Defects for Weighted Potential Systems
abstract: In this paper, we consider \[ \begin{cases} u=K*(|x|^αa_0(x)v^p)&\quad\hbox{in }\mathbb R^n,\\ v=K*(|x|^βb_0(x)u^q)&\quad\hbox{in }\mathbb R^n, \end{cases} \] where $n\ge2$, $0<ρ<n$, $p,q>0$, and $α,β>-ρ$. The radial kernel is nonincreasing and satisfies $K(r)\asymp r^{ρ-n}$. The coefficients satisfy $0<c_0\le a_0(x),b_0(x)\le C_0$ and $|x|(|\nabla\log a_0(x)|+|\nabla\log b_0(x)|)\le L$. We prove nonexistence if \[ \frac{n+α-\varepsilon_a}{p+1} +\frac{n+β-\varepsilon_b}{q+1}>n-ρ+\varepsilon_K, \] where the defects bound the radial logarithmic derivatives. No symmetry, finite-energy condition, or prescribed decay is assumed. The proof combines a localized virial identity with a source-layer pressure estimate whose constants are uniform under centered dilations, including the low-order range $0<ρ\le1$. We also identify the necessary scaling range for existence. For radial weighted Newton systems with unequal powers, we prove that the combined coefficient defect has a sharp, unattained infimum equal to the subcritical gap. A fixed bound on the coefficient ratios forces a strictly larger defect, whereas suitable coefficient--solution pairs approach the threshold with excess at most $C/\log M$. In the scalar Newton case, the threshold is explicit and the approximating family converges, after normalization, to an explicit critical weighted profile. The sharpness results concern the Newton kernel; no corresponding construction is asserted for general fractional kernels.

title: A cosmic filament catalog for COSMOS-Web Data Release 1 across 0.5 < z < 3.5
abstract: Cosmic filaments represent the environments in which most galaxies form and evolve. However, the spatial distribution of filaments and the link between galaxy properties and their positions relative to filaments remains unclear, particularly at high redshifts. In this work, using the deep-field catalog COSMOS-Web Data Release 1, we construct a filament catalog spanning 0.5 < z < 3.5 that can be directly applied to studies of galaxy evolution and the galaxy--large-scale-structure connection at the peak epoch of galaxy and black hole formation. We developed a new procedure based on the DisPerSE method that fully incorporates the probability distribution functions (PDFs) of galaxy photometric redshifts by generating multiple realizations for each tomographic 2D slice. We then stacked these realizations to construct ``filament probability maps'' (w_ fil maps), from which filaments were subsequently extracted. The filament extraction parameters were optimized using mock catalogs generated from TNG simulations by minimizing the discrepancies between 3D and projected 2D filaments. Applying this procedure to the COSMOS-Web data, we detected 12,523 filaments (comprising 136,210 segments) across 0.5 < z < 3.5 and released a filament catalog, a companion segment catalog, and filament probability maps for each slice. Validation against astrophysical properties shows a strong agreement between the extracted filaments and those in the simulations, supporting the robustness of the filament extraction. These data products provide a robust foundation for investigating galaxy--environment coevolution at cosmic noon and beyond.

title: SARIA: Persistence-Aware KV Caching with Coordinated DRAM--SSD Reload for LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-turn LLM agents usually reuse long context prefixes, making key value (KV) caching crucial for reducing prefill latency. SSDs provide a low-cost extension to limited DRAM capacity but introduce two key challenges. Eagerly persisting all KV cache blocks incurs substantial write traffic and rapidly consumes finite SSD endurance. Meanwhile, the small number of SSDs provisioned in typical GPU servers limits aggregate reload bandwidth, making SSD-resident KV cache much slower to retrieve than that in DRAM and inflating prefill latency. We present \textsc{Saria} (Selective Admission and Reload for Inference Acceleration), a KV caching system that jointly manages DRAM and SSD by exploiting the session-level temporal locality of LLM agents to reduce SSD writes and accelerate cache reload. On the write path, \textsc{Saria} uses eviction and reuse history to selectively persist KV cache blocks that exhibit reuse opportunities beyond their DRAM residency, avoiding unnecessary writes for KV cache already hosted in DRAM. On the read path, \textsc{Saria} promotes selected SSD-hit KV cache blocks from GPU memory into DRAM after prefill, allowing subsequent reuse within the same session to reduce SSD read traffic while limiting DRAM contention. A transfer coordinator paces DRAM reads while SSD transfers are active, allowing both paths to make progress and efficiently share GPU ingress bandwidth. We implement \textsc{Saria} on LMCache MP and evaluate it using workloads from TraceLab and WEKA, covering both full-attention and hybrid-attention models. The results show that \textsc{Saria} reduces SSD writes by 57.1--58.9\% compared with popular full duplicate caching and the mean time to first token (TTFT) by 42.3--79.7\% over DRAM-only caching.

title: Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent
abstract: We propose Quantum Constrained Hamiltonian Descent (QCHD), a continuous-time quantum framework for optimization under smooth equality constraints. The unconstrained counterpart, Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), minimizes a cost function by simulating the Schrödinger dynamics of a particle in the potential given by the cost function. Applying Dirac's formalism to the classical dynamics with constraints, we construct an intrinsic quantum Hamiltonian with a Laplace--Beltrami operator on the constraint manifold in a kinetic term. Its evolution preserves the constraints exactly without penalty terms and is expected to solve quantum-dynamically the constrained optimization problem. We analyze its relation to Quantum Hamiltonian Descent supplemented by a strong penalty term. For a squared-distance penalty, the effective tangential dynamics acquires an extrinsic-curvature potential and, in nontrivial normal-rotation sectors, a coupling to the normal-bundle connection. These embedding-dependent terms remain in the strong-penalty limit, generally yielding quantum dynamics different from QCHD. Numerical comparisons for circular, elliptical, and two simultaneous constraints show faster optimization and improved concentration near global minima for the initial states and finite penalty strengths considered.

title: Optimal Hardy weights for the fractional discrete Dirichlet Laplacian on the half-line
abstract:
For positive powers of the discrete Dirichlet Laplacian $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$, non-trivial Hardy weights exist if and only if $0<σ<3/2$. For $0<σ\leq 1$, an explicit optimal Hardy weight for $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$ was obtained by Das and de la Fuente-Fernández. Their ground state argument does not apply when $1<σ<3/2$, because the off-diagonal matrix entries of $(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ$ are no longer all non-positive. Nevertheless, we show that their result is true for the entire subcriticality range $0<σ<3/2$. For $1<σ<3/2$, our argument combines the factorisation $$(-Δ_{\mathrm{D}})^σ=
abla_{\mathrm{D}}^{*}(-Δ_{\mathrm{N}})^{σ-1}
abla_{\mathrm{D}},$$ where $
abla_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $-Δ_{\mathrm{N}}$ are the discrete Dirichlet gradient and the discrete Neumann Laplacian, respectively, with a suitable two-term ground state representation. In addition, we use these arguments to derive another explicit family of optimal Hardy weights for any $σ\in(0,3/2)$.

title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.

title: On the arithmetic Siegel--Weil formula for orthogonal Shimura varieties over a general totally real field
abstract: Let $\mathrm{F}/\mathbb{Q}_p$ be a finite extension with $p\ne 2$, and let $V$ be a quadratic space over $\mathrm{F}$ of dimension at least two admitting a self-dual lattice. We prove the local arithmetic Siegel-Weil formula for GSpin Rapoport-Zink spaces formulated by Li and Zhang. We use the global-to-local strategy of Mihatsch and Zhang and its application by Luo. Using a generalization of the prismatic realization functor of Imai, Kato, and Youcis, we construct and study derived special cycles on integral models of SO Shimura varieties and their Rapoport-Zink uniformizations. We derive the local intersection formula from the modularity of special cycles on the generic fiber. As a first application, we prove the corresponding semi-global arithmetic Siegel-Weil identity for orthogonal Shimura varieties over a totally real field $F\ne\mathbb{Q}$.

title: An elementary proof of rational injectivity in equivariant KK-theory
abstract: Antonini, Azzali and Skandalis proved that, for every countable discrete group $Γ$, the canonical map $EΓ\to\underline{E}Γ$ induces a split injection in equivariant $KK$-theory with real coefficients. In this paper, we give a more elementary proof of the corresponding rational injectivity result in ordinary equivariant $KK$-theory without using $\mathrm{II}_1$ factors.

title: Robust paths to primordial $B$ modes in the presence of polarised point source contamination
abstract: A detection of primordial $B$ modes in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarisation relies on a robust control and removal of contamination from astrophysical polarised foreground emission. We examine how much polarised extragalactic point sources may contaminate the cosmological signal in ground-based CMB experiments, propagating their impact through component separation to the final parameter constraints. We discuss masking and modelling strategies to ensure that the resulting constraints remain both accurate and precise under this source of contamination. We produce synthetic data containing polarised emission from extragalactic radio sources (ERSs) and dusty star-forming galaxies (DSFGs) following state-of-the-art models for both samples. We find that, while the DSFG contribution is likely too small to cause any significant bias to the cosmological or foreground parameters, the ERS contribution instead, if left unmasked, leads to a bias in the parameters describing the Galactic synchrotron and lensing $B$-mode components. For experiments targeting noise levels of order $σ_P\simeq 1\,μK\,{\rm arcmin}$, we find that masking all ERSs with fluxes above $\sim$0.1 Jy, coupled with a relatively simple model to marginalise over residual point-source contamination, achieves a suitable balance that allows for the robust recovery of unbiased cosmological and foreground parameters at a negligible cost in parameter uncertainties.

title: Tracking the Emergence and Persistence of Abnormal Grain Growth in an Aluminum Alloy using Diffraction-Contrast Tomography
abstract: Abnormal grain growth is inherently three-dimensional, making 3D tracking of grain evolution essential for understanding its underlying mechanisms. This study combines synchrotron-based diffraction-contrast tomography and phase-contrast tomography to characterize the three-dimensional grain structure and quantify the size and spatial distribution of second-phase particles in the aluminum alloy AA5252. Using an interrupted annealing protocol, we tracked the persistent growth of abnormal grains and the emergence of abnormal growth in a grain initially belonging to the matrix. Although second-phase particles effectively suppressed grain growth in the matrix, variations in local particle density showed no apparent correlation with either the emergence or subsequent rapid growth of abnormal grains. Instead, crystallographic misorientation and, more notably, neighboring grain size were identified as stronger predictors of abnormal growth rate. Matrix grains were consumed more rapidly when they were relatively small and shared high-angle grain boundaries with the growing abnormal grain. The same trends were observed for the grain that underwent a transition from normal to abnormal growth. Remarkably, even before the onset of abnormal growth, this grain was surrounded by smaller matrix grains with exclusively high-angle grain boundaries, while the local particle density was slightly higher than average. These findings suggest that the same microstructural characteristics facilitate both the emergence and persistence of abnormal grain growth, although the mechanism triggering the transition to rapid growth remains unresolved.

title: Gravitational waves from highly charged binary black holes in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton theory
abstract: We perform fully nonlinear numerical-relativity simulations of electrically charged binary black hole mergers in Einstein-Maxwell-dilaton (EMD) theory, varying the magnitude and relative sign of the input charges and the dilaton coupling $a$. In the weak-charge sequence, the dominant gravitational waveforms remain close to the neutral vacuum baseline of general relativity and are visually indistinguishable across the sampled couplings, consistent with earlier EMD simulations. For the highly charged binaries with equal-magnitude opposite charges, however, the dominant gravitational strain exhibits visible differences between the EMD cases with $a\neq0$ and the charged Einstein-Maxwell reference at $a=0$. At $a=1$, the coordinate-time interval from the same separation to the waveform-based merger is approximately $62\%$ shorter than for the neutral binary. In this high-charge sequence at fixed input charges, increasing $a$ strengthens the scalar dressing while leaving the individual dilaton-weighted horizon charges nearly unchanged. Within the same sequence, increasing $a$ across the sampled values decreases the dipolar electromagnetic-flux peak, increases the scalar-flux peak, and modestly lengthens the merger interval. The sampled like-charged binaries have corresponding merger intervals approximately $15\%$-$20\%$ longer than the neutral baseline and emit predominantly quadrupolar electromagnetic radiation. At $a=1$ and $a=\sqrt{3}$, the like-charged mergers leave charged remnants with scalar fields consistent with secondary dilaton hair. The opposite-charge remnants instead approach neutral black holes without stationary scalar hair.

title: BelT Block Cipher
abstract: BelT is a block cipher with a 128-bit block size and a 256-bit key, developed in Belarus and adopted as part of the Belarusian national standard STB 34.101.31 for encryption and integrity control. Its specification was issued as a preliminary standard in 2007, becoming a final standard in 2011. BelT employs an eight-round structure combining elements of a Feistel network and the Lai-Massey scheme. This paper presents a complete description of the cipher and explains the principles underlying its design. Software performance and possible optimizations of BelT are discussed in comparison with those of candidates in the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition.

title: Degenerations of Jordan algebras
abstract: We describe all degenerations of complex $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras and of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras. The proofs do not use other papers on degenerations, and all degenerations and non-degenerations were formally verified in the proof assistant Lean~4. The graph of primary degenerations of $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras has $73$ vertices and $160$ edges. The variety of $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras is stratified into $63$ normal forms, five of which are one- or two-parameter families; together with two special members of a family this gives $65$ objects, and the graph of primary degenerations has $154$ edges. In particular, we describe all irreducible components of the corresponding varieties: the variety of $4$-dimensional Jordan algebras has $10$ irreducible components, and the variety of $5$-dimensional nilpotent Jordan algebras has dimension $22$ and $5$ irreducible components.

title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
abstract: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.

title: A cosmological intercept tension in local distance ladders
abstract: The Hubble tension motivates direct tests of the internal consistency of the local distance ladder. We perform forward and backward consistency checks between Type Ia supernovae in Cepheid host galaxies and the Hubble-flow supernova sample using Pantheon+ data. Within flat $Λ$CDM, we impose Planck-CMB priors on one sample, infer the supernova absolute-magnitude calibration, and propagate it to the other sample to recover the Hubble constant, which should match the input value if the second and third rungs of the distance ladder align perfectly. We examine the impact of host-galaxy peculiar velocities using redshift corrections based on the Manticore-Local reconstruction. These corrections shift the recovered $H_0$ from $74.30^{+1.18}_{-1.20}$ to $71.37^{+1.23}_{-1.18}$ $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ in the forward analysis and from $60.83^{+0.98}_{-0.97}$ to $63.25^{+0.95}_{-0.93}$ $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ in the backward analysis, bringing both results closer to the input CMB constraint. Comparing the cosmological intercepts of the magnitude-redshift relation inferred from two rungs of the distance ladder before and after peculiar-velocity corrections, we find that the significance of the discrepancy decreases from $6.8σ$ to $3.9σ$ in the forward check and from $7.3σ$ to $4.3σ$ in the backward check. Peculiar-velocity corrections therefore partially alleviate the intercept tension, while a residual discrepancy persists within the adopted framework. Our results highlight the importance of local velocity modeling and motivate further tests of sample selection and calibration systematics in assessing distance-ladder consistency.

title: The XMM-Newton view of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
abstract: We present the first multi-wavelength analysis of the DEM L36 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud. We compare the DEM L36 superbubble with other Galactic and Magellanic Cloud superbubbles. We use data from XMM-Newton, supplemented by data from the Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Dark Energy Camera Magellanic Cloud Emission Line Survey, the Spitzer Space Telescope, and the Australia Telescope Compact Array. We perform a multi-wavelength morphological analysis to understand the shape and structure of the superbubble and X-ray spectral analysis to derive physical parameters of the hot gas. We find significant X-ray emission in DEM L36, dominated by a central bubble region mostly confined by a thin H$α$ filamentary shell. This has two distinct blowout regions to the east and west, with a possible smaller blowout in the south. Spectral analysis shows the X-ray emission is well fit with a thermal plasma model in collisional ionisation equilibrium with a temperature of $kT=0.17~(0.16-0.18)$ keV and unabsorbed luminosity $L_{X~(0.5-7.0~\mathrm{keV})}=3.62\times 10^{35} $erg s$^{-1}$. Unlike other LMC superbubbles, we find no clear powering cluster at the centre, though relatively small clusters near the edge are likely supplying the mechanical input at the present epoch. We use photometric data of these clusters to estimate cluster masses, ages, and mechanical inputs to compare with the energy stored in the superbubble. We find that these clusters have supplied more energy over their lifetime than is currently observed in the superbubble, indicative of the so-called growth rate discrepancy problem. It is likely the DEM L36 superbubble was initially shaped by a central massive stellar population that has since dispersed and largely lost to supernovae, with smaller clusters at the edges of the swept-up shell being currently supplying the energy input.

title: Unconstrained learning of equivariant atomistic properties
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have made first-principles accuracy routine for the potential energy surface (PES). Their backbones, often O(3)-equivariant by design, are increasingly used to learn other atomistic properties. Many of these are of high angular order or pseudotensorial character, defined per atom, or expanded on large atom-centered basis sets. Such targets strain equivariant GNNs, whose tensor products grow steeply in cost with angular order and can fail to represent the target if truncated, forcing difficult trade-offs between hyperparameters. Unconstrained models like the Point-Edge Transformer (PET) instead replace explicit O(3) algebra with edge-to-edge attention and learn equivariance from data, so that the same backbone can in principle learn any equivariant property. We demonstrate how to use PET to learn molecular dipoles and polarizabilities, NMR chemical shielding tensors, and auxiliary-basis expansions of the electron density. Increasing the backbone size systematically improves both accuracy and equivariance error, and targeted architectural and training choices reduce the symmetry breaking further. PET matches or improves on the released reference models at lower inference cost and, compared with equivariant models, a smaller memory footprint. The predictions give accurate IR and Raman spectra and isotropic shieldings; the predicted densities accelerate self-consistent field calculations and give one-shot ground-state properties, and pretrained density models transfer to higher levels of theory by fine-tuning on little data. The impact of approximate equivariance is small for most observables, further validating this approach to train fast, accurate, and useful surrogate models for properties beyond the PES.

title: Anomalous polar chains in halide perovskites
abstract: Local polar distortions, their collective ordering, and their field-driven reversal have been studied extensively in ferroelectric perovskites for decades. Here we identify an unusual behavior in the ferroelectric halide perovskite CsGeBr3 using large-scale molecular dynamics with first-principles-trained interatomic potentials. In its nominally cubic phase the Ge off-centering forms one-dimensional polar chains that extend over at least tens of nanometers and relax on nanosecond timescales, four orders of magnitude slower than in BaTiO3 and PbTiO3, with CsSnBr3 in between. The cubic CsGeBr3 phase is a dynamically disordered state in which oppositely polarized chains flip throughout the crystal, and a long-lived one-dimensional local polarization coexists with zero net polarization. A simple three-dimensional perovskite thus hosts long-ranged one-dimensional polar correlations with remarkably slow dynamics. In the ferroelectric phase the same chains set a one-dimensional switching mechanism, in which the polarization reverses chain by chain.

title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.

title: RaSFNet: Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network for LiDAR Semantic Segmentation
abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.

title: Entanglement certification of attosecond light fields with photoelectron interferometry
abstract: The emergence of entangled quantum optical states in high-harmonic generation raises a fundamental problem about its characterization, namely, \textit{how can entanglement of extreme-ultraviolet radiation be certified for attosecond light fields?} Here, we provide experimentally accessible separability tests, particularly showing that attosecond photoelectron interferometry provides a direct solution to this problem. This is achieved by a quantum optical treatment of mapping photoelectron interferometry to the measurement of optical correlation functions. This yields a negative-partial-transpose witness for infrared-XUV entanglement and a sufficient witness of genuine multipartite entanglement without auxiliary optical measurements. We evaluate both witnesses on explicit optical states and identify how the protocol can be extended to XUV-XUV entanglement certification. Hence, we establish attosecond photoelectron interferometry as a general framework for entanglement certification across a wide range of optical frequencies.

title: ChainSEED: A Scalable, High-Fidelity Blockchain Emulator
abstract: Researchers need blockchain experimental environments with configurable workloads, controllable network conditions, and observable outcomes. Public blockchains and testnets limit experimental control, model-based simulators omit real client implementations, and real-client environments face challenges in combining network control with resource-efficient deployment. We present ChainSEED, a scalable, high-fidelity blockchain emulator built on the SEED Internet Emulator. It separates blockchain configuration from client placement on a configurable routed network. For Ethereum PoS, it organizes separately configured execution, consensus, and validator clients and provides APIs for customizing genesis state, peer connections, and client software. A transaction generator informed by Ethereum mainnet activity, application interfaces, and chain- and node-level monitoring support experiments. ChainSEED also supports Monero and Solana. We examine beacon-node memory reduction, execution-client memory allocation, and validator-client multiplexing to support larger experiments within limited hardware budgets. On a single server with approximately 1 TiB of memory and 384 logical CPU cores, ChainSEED deploys 400 beacon nodes, 400 execution nodes, and 60,000 validator identities while sustaining approximately 20 TPS. It also emulates a 1,200-node Monero network with up to 200 active single-threaded PoW miners and a 200-node Solana network with sustained finalization. Case studies demonstrate routing attacks, blockchain amplification attacks, Monero eclipse attacks, topology-discovery benchmarking against known peer graphs, and network-configuration experiments.

title: Holographic surface defect RG flows without supersymmetry
abstract: We consider $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang--Mills theory with gauge group SU$(N)$, which admits families of conformal surface defects defined by singular boundary conditions for scalar fields that completely break supersymmetry. At large $N$ and strong coupling, these defects are holographically dual either to a probe D5-brane or to one of two new D7-brane embeddings that we introduce in this work. We also construct embeddings of both D5- and D7-branes describing defect renormalisation group (RG) flows, for which the ultraviolet and infrared fixed points are both dual to the same D$p$-brane, with different values of a parameter. Our embeddings dual to RG flows are mostly constructed numerically, but we find a regime in which we can derive approximate analytic embeddings using a controlled perturbative expansion. We demonstrate that the $b$-theorem is satisfied by all of the RG flows that we study.

title: Site and bond percolation thresholds of all $k$-uniform tilings with $k\le 10$
abstract: We determine the site and bond percolation thresholds of all 23,396 $k$-uniform tilings of the plane by regular polygons with $k\le 10$, the complete set according to the known enumeration. We use Monte Carlo simulation on tori and the condition that no wrapping and a cross-wrapping cluster are equally probable, the Monte Carlo form of the critical-polynomial criterion, which needs no knowledge of the large-scale anisotropy that most of these lattices have. The 486 thresholds with $k\le4$ have uncertainties of a few units in the sixth decimal and reproduce the 22 Archimedean reference values (rms deviation 0.71 standard errors) and unpublished bond thresholds of the 20 two-uniform lattices ($χ^2=19.5$ for 20 values); the others have median statistical uncertainties of $2\times10^{-5}$ ($k\le7$) to $7\times10^{-5}$ ($k\ge8$) and no detectable finite-size bias. The vertex-type fractions alone fix the thresholds for $k\ge5$ to about $2\times10^{-3}$ (linear rule fitted on $k\le4$), while tilings with equal composition differ by up to $6\times10^{-3}$ (site) and $2\times10^{-2}$ (bond). In the range of domain sizes covered, descriptors of radius one account for more than half of this difference, and stackings of identical strips have thresholds linear in the fraction of each boundary type. For tilings that differ only by the registry of strips separated by $h$ rows of squares, the bond threshold difference decreases by a factor of 6-8 per row, comparable to the leading momentum-$π$ eigenvalue of the square-band transfer matrix.

title: Timelike Supersymmetric Geometries in Seven-Dimensional Supergravity
abstract: Seven-dimensional supergravity poses a uniquely intricate supersymmetry problem, combining topologically massive higher-form gauge dynamics, distinct Clifford algebra properties, and rich geometric structures. We first establish the complete formulation of the maximal Cartan-gauged theory in terms of the gauge-invariant higher-form flux, including both the bosonic action and supersymmetry variations. This formulation, which also makes the smooth ungauged limit manifest, is achieved by requiring a consistent truncation to the minimal Cartan-gauged theory in the equal-charge limit. We construct the complete bilinear system for a timelike Killing vector, where additional internal orientation of the symplectic-Majorana spinor arises already in the scalar sector, uniquely among pure minimal ungauged theories. In the equal-charge sector, we decouple the algebraic constraints into SU$(3)$-isotypic components, and analyse the differential bilinear relations, determining the permitted dilaton gradient, fluxes, fibration twist and intrinsic torsion of the base. We prove that with gauging and active Cartan flux, the complex scalar bilinear vanishes identically. We also construct a Killing gauge for the higher-form potential compatible with the self-duality condition. We show that with gauging but no active Cartan flux, the Killing vector also acts as a generator of the gauged R-symmetry, and the base structure is enlarged from SU$(3)$ to U$(3)$. We find that BPS-flow solutions realize this setting. With supersymmetry, we isolate a single independent component of the 3-form equation across an exhaustive four-class partition for both theories within this setup. Applied to known and proposed solutions in both theories, this classification exposes unexplored sectors and provides an accessible toolbox for constructing and testing solutions and developing new geometric and holographic applications.

title: Large Language Models Meet Bayesian Optimization: Towards Self-evolving Wireless Digital Twins
abstract: Wireless digital twins (DTs) are increasingly integrated with artificial intelligence to support online modeling, prediction, and network optimization. However, most existing approaches perform adaptation within predefined learning or optimization structures, which may become unsuitable when wireless tasks and operating conditions change. In this article, we investigate the integration of large language models (LLMs) and Bayesian optimization (BO) to extend wireless DTs from online adaptation towards algorithm-level self-evolution. We introduce an LLM-assisted BO framework in which BO provides a stable and sample-efficient optimization backbone, while the LLM determines whether selected BO components should be retained or adapted based on the current task and accumulated optimization experience. In simulations, we apply the framework to Gaussian process (GP) kernel discovery for a multi-user wireless beam-selection problem. Simulation results show that the LLM-discovered kernel improves the final BO performance by 19.7% on the training tasks compared with the strongest standard kernel baseline. The results demonstrate the potential of combining LLM flexibility with structured BO for self-evolving wireless DTs.

title: When More Metadata Misleads: Probing Field-Level Grounding in LLM-Generated Museum Descriptions
abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.

title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

title: Constrained Sparsest Input Selection for Structural Controllability is NP-Hard
abstract: We study the problem of selecting the fewest admissible input--state links that make a structured linear system structurally controllable. This objective counts nonzero entries from prescribed positions of the input matrix and is different from minimizing its number of nonzero columns. Prior work gives polynomial-time algorithms for several restricted cases, including single or dedicated inputs and prescribed input patterns satisfying additional graph-theoretic conditions. We give a polynomial-time reduction from perfect three-dimensional matching, establishing for the first time that the decision problem is NP-complete and the optimization problem is NP-hard. A refinement of the reduction yields an exact optimum relation and shows that the problem is APX-hard. An example also exhibits a strict integrality gap for the natural linear programming relaxation.

title: Structural cryptanalysis of classic McEliece: Assessment of claims, costs and evidence
abstract: For the last two years, classical structural attacks on McEliece with binary Goppa codes progressed further, at the parameters of Classic McEliece, than in the previous four decades: a subexponential and then a quasi-polynomial distinguisher, key recoveries for public challenges with brute-force labels up to $254$, and conditional key-recovery estimates of about $2^{89}$ to $2^{128}$ per run of a large sparse linear-algebra computation, depending on the parameter set and on whether and how memory access is charged. On September 2026 the German BSI advised against new deployments of the scheme. This paper gives a version-aware critical assessment of these results. It separates proved distinguishers, conditional cost estimates and actual recoveries; analyses in detail Saarinen's HOVER algorithm, his conditional cost analysis and his recovery of the TII-254 challenge, together with Weis's cost study of Holdout/Hermite key recovery; and compares the other key-recovery routes and the objections raised against them. Our own analysis finds that the cost model is now the main quantitative uncertainty, with about thirty bits between the cheapest and the most expensive model for the same computation; that for the four larger parameter sets every model considered leaves the conditional estimates far below the targeted levels, whereas for mceliece348864 the shortfall is of the order of the spread between models; that the structural estimates are lower than Grover-accelerated information-set decoding for the four larger sets in essentially every model and comparable for mceliece348864; and that none of this is a demonstrated attack, since the underlying heuristics have been tested only on instances tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of times smaller than the target. We close with open questions.

title: String Amplitudes on Integer Rectangles
abstract: Hidden zeros of tree-level string amplitudes of colored scalars lie on loci specified by integer-valued dimensionless momentum contractions arranged in rectangles on the kinematic mesh. We study the same kinematic loci for open-string amplitudes with gluons, fermions and higher-spin states at arbitrary finite mass levels. Disk monodromy relations yield $\textit{zero-locus factorization}$: at regular points where the monodromy system is invertible, the amplitude is a weighted sum of physical three-point amplitudes sewn to complete on-shell $(n-1)$-point amplitudes. Hidden zeros follow when the external wavefunctions annihilate all contributing three-point couplings. In the low-energy limit, the massless zero-integer branch recovers the corresponding field-theory factorization. For closed strings, including gravitons, persistent cubic zeros in both chiral sectors remove the disk poles, allowing the Kawai--Lewellen--Tye momentum-kernel zero to imply amplitude zeros. The operator product expansions of external vertices give a common worldsheet origin for these conditions across spins and mass levels.

title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.

title: Investigating Multi-Cultural Value Selection Biases in LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) serve users whose cultural identities are multi-layered, yet cultural evaluations commonly reduce identity to one label. In this work, we study LLMs under simultaneous identity cues, with a country persona in the system prompt and a second identity signaled in the user turn, either by naming a country (explicit cue) or through the query language (implicit cue). We test World Values Survey (WVS) multiple-choice probing and open-ended sociopolitical generation. In multiple-choice probing, language cues shift answers about three times more than explicit cues but away from the associated country's distribution, and explicit cues do not consistently move answers toward the named country. Across 1.6 million open-ended responses, naming a country closes 30-44% of the gap to the model's own responses for that country, and explicit cues produce more differentiated value changes than language cues. Our results suggest that country and language cues should be evaluated as distinct signals rather than interchangeable proxies for culture.

title: Eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems
abstract: We have identified numerous triply eclipsing hierarchical triple star systems from observations made with the space telescope TESS. For many of these systems we can potentially determine their dynamical and astrophysical parameters with high precision, in some cases even without the use of radial velocity data. In the present paper we report the comprehensive study of eight new, triply eclipsing triple star systems, taken from this larger sample: TICs 77177148, 220456364, 232874003, 306690194, 343763382, 358795247, 379084660, 385933895. Besides the photometric data from the TESS observations, we obtained supplementary ground-based photometric measurements, as well as radial velocity measurements for some of the systems. The eclipse timing variation curves extracted from the TESS data and from the ground-based follow up data, the photometric light curves, radial velocity data, and the spectral energy distribution are combined in a complex photodynamical analysis to yield the stellar and orbital parameters for all of the investigated systems. The outer periods are in the range of 63-294 days, including the currently sixth tightest known triple system, TI 385933895 with an outer to inner period ratio of 9.82. We find that all of the triples are nearly coplanar, with mutual inclination angles of <=2.5deg. Despite such flatness, we still detect eclipse depth variations in TIC 220456364 that are induced by orbital plane precession. Moreover, we find that TIC 358795247 is likely a (2+1)+1-type hierarchical quadruple system. Finally we make some statistical assessments of a number of the orbital elements, stellar parameters, and distances of these systems.

title: The Reversible Intermediate Language L4, its Type System, and its Bidirectional Small-Step Semantics
abstract: L4 is a generic, reversible, linearly-typed, low-level language intended as an intermediate language for compiling reversible programming languages to reversible machines. L4 is intended to replace and generalise RSSA, a reversible SSA form. Inspiration is drawn from other low-level reversible languages such as HSSA. In this paper, we define L4 first informally, and then give a formal type system and a bidirectional small-step semantics for L4: The rules have direction indicators to determine forwards or backwards execution, and the direction can be changed during execution.

title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

title: Almost tight distributed approximation for domination in sparse graph classes
abstract: We study distributed approximation of Minimum Dominating Set in a very general class of sparse graphs, extending near-optimal approximation results from the minor-free setting to bounded expansion. In more detail, for fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we give a new deterministic constant-round LOCAL algorithm for Minimum Dominating Set on graphs of maximum average degree at most $d$ and bounded depth-one shallow-minor density. Its approximation ratio is $d+1+\varepsilon$, which is optimal up to $\varepsilon$ for every even integer $d\geq 2$. This improves on the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz by extending beyond proper minor-closed classes. From this algorithm, we derive almost-tight constant-round approximations for a number of graph classes. We get $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximations for planar graphs and graphs of bounded Euler genus, and $(5+\varepsilon)$-approximations for their triangle-free subclasses. This answers the $7+\varepsilon$ question of Wawrzyniak positively, and matches the recent results of Amiri and Siebertz. We also apply our algorithm to classes of bounded queue-number or stack-number, obtaining bounds that are tight up to $\varepsilon$. Additionally, we answer questions of Amiri and Siebertz about improving the dependence of the round complexity on $1/\varepsilon$ and obtaining polynomial local computation for fixed parameters, when comparing the output to the usual domination number.

title: Feeder-Aware Service-Conditioned Flexibility of Grid-Interactive Buildings
abstract: Grid-interactive buildings can adjust demand, but building-feasible power budgets may differ from accepted feeder-head offers. This study addresses a practical question: to what extent can the adjustable electricity consumption of buildings be translated into deliverable flexibility services while satisfying feeder-head operating requirements? To enable a fair comparison, we adopt the same baseline operating schedule, equipment conditions, and post-service recovery requirements for indoor temperature and battery state of charge (SOC). Flexibility is then evaluated under two settings: one considering only building-level constraints, and the other additionally accounting for feeder-head constraints. We first use a simplified network model with explicit security margins to determine a preliminary amount of flexibility that can be committed. The resulting schedule is then validated using a more detailed network simulation via Modelica. If network losses cause the actual response to deviate from the committed response, the electricity consumption of individual buildings is rescheduled. If the required response still cannot be achieved, the committed flexibility level is reduced. The experiments cover multiple service activation times, regulation directions, and service durations. For comparative purposes, we retain the initial optimization result as the reference estimate of the maximum potentially available flexibility, rather than interpreting the failure of a particular subsequent realization attempt as evidence that a larger flexibility level is inherently infeasible. The results demonstrated that 24.51\% of nonzero flexibility contracts were rejected due to feeder-head constraints, 67.04\% of contracts were accepted with some rescheduling and building redispatch, and only 8.09\% of contracts were accepted without any changes.

title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

title: Mn-deficient Ni-Mn-Ga alloys: phase transitions, magnetic properties, and disappearance of martensitic transformation
abstract: Composition gradients formed during directional solidification are generally considered undesirable in Ni-Mn-Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys. However, these gradients offer a highly effective platform for systematically investigating composition-property relationships under identical growth and heat-treatment conditions.
