abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

title: VTRL-Med: Progressive Visual Refinement with Topology-Guided Regularization for Medical Image Clustering
abstract: Deep clustering offers a promising approach for analyzing large unlabeled medical image datasets, yet prevailing methods still face two limitations: they may neglect class-agnostic structural priors that capture object boundaries and regions, and they do not explicitly encode topological patterns (e.g., connectivity and holes). These sources of information play distinct and complementary roles: visual-structural features provide the primary discriminative representation for clustering, while topological features provide additional global geometric cues for residual visual ambiguities. We introduce VTRL-Med, a progressive visual-structural learning framework with topology-guided regularization for medical image clustering. VTRL-Med first adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to extract image features that retain structural cues inherited from mask-supervised pretraining. It then generates reliable pseudo-labels through a two-step filtering process that combines prototype-based selection with k-nearest neighbor consistency validation. Finally, it progressively refines the visual branch while an auxiliary topology branch, constructed from persistent homology (PH) descriptors, provides additional geometric regularization during training. Across 13 medical image benchmarks, VTRL-Med achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance, improving average accuracy by 4.48% over existing methods. On three representative datasets, topology-guided regularization further improves accuracy by 1.3--4.3% over visual refinement alone.

title: Polarization-encoded photon statistics for counting dipole emitters
abstract: Counting the emitters within a diffraction-limited region is a prerequisite for localizing overlapping molecules. Under pulsed excitation, each molecule emits at most one photon per pulse, so photon-number-resolved detection can count emitters without resolving them. But the required number of pulses grows steeply with the emitter number. Here we show that polarization, conventionally used to measure the orientations of dipole emitters, also carries information on their number. Because mean polarization-resolved signals are unchanged when every emitter is replaced by multiple dimmer copies, this information resides in the photon statistics within each pulse, which polarization reshapes in two ways. Linearly polarized excitation at three angles increases the sub-Poissonian deficit of the photon count by a factor of 1.5 for any emitter orientation, and detection in four polarization channels reveals the emitter number through how the photons of multiphoton pulses are distributed among the channels. Maximum-likelihood simulations for two to five emitters of unknown orientations and brightnesses show that three-angle excitation reduces the required number of pulses by about 2.3-fold, close to the predicted $1.5^2=2.25$, and that adding four-channel detection raises the reduction to as much as 4.8-fold. These gains require only polarization optics added to photon-number-resolved detection.

title: Sobolev inequalities for sections and projections of log-concave functions
abstract: Higher order sharp Sobolev and local Sobolev type inequalities for log-concave functions are established. The new inequalities directly imply the isoperimetric inequalities by Bollobás and Thomason in 1995, by Liakopoulos in 2019, and the recently discovered local isoperimetric inequalities from [1]. In order to do so, we make use of three ingredients. First, sets of functional inequalities proven by Alonso-Gutiérrez, Bernués, Brazitikos and Carbery in 2021. Second, a multidimensional polynomial optimization result that originated in [1] and was initiated by Bollobás and Thomason. Third, a new integral formula for the projection of a log-concave function that links the geometric part with the more functional versions via some dependence on the Hessian matrix restricted to subspaces.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Transition Predictions: A Bellman Theory
abstract: Multi-step predictions of future transition realizations can improve reinforcement learning, but their value remains difficult to quantify. Directly including these predictions in the state can lead to exponential state-space growth, making direct dynamic programming computationally expensive. We study discounted finite MDPs under a block-feedback protocol: at the start of each K-period block, the decision maker observes $K$-step probabilistic transition predictions for a subset of actions and adapts decisions to observed states within the block. We show that the optimal value satisfies a Bayesian Bellman equation on the original state space. This representation reveals that predictive information creates value by recursively changing the local order of maximization and expectation in the Bellman expansion. We formalize this effect through a Bellman--Jensen analysis and quantify the effects of prediction horizon, error, action coverage, and within-block feedback. We propose block-feedback Bayesian offline learning with online adaptation (BF--BOLA), a model-based algorithm for learning near-optimal policies, and establish upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that match up to logarithmic factors in the stated regimes. The results show that predictions can reduce transition learning to uncovered rows and that learning a near-optimal policy can require fewer prediction samples than estimating the Bayesian value function.

title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.

title: Reducing 6G Energy Consumption: TDD-Aligned Drain Voltage Modulation for Power Amplifiers
abstract: The Power Amplifier (PA) of a base station operates inefficiently at partial load, where back-off from the peak output power wastes supply headroom. Adapting the PA drain voltage to the instantaneous signal recovers this loss but requires frequent switching, increasing hardware cost. We propose TDD-Aligned Drain Voltage Modulation (TDD-DVM), a drain voltage modulation scheme that instead selects the drain voltage level once per Time-Division Duplex (TDD) period based on the downlink resource load and switches the voltage during the uplink window. This is enabled by the authors' previous work on POLITE link adaptation, which spreads the transmit power over resources left unused at partial load and moves the PA into a regime where a lower drain voltage suffices. In a 3GPP Urban Macro system-level simulation across traffic loads, we compare TDD-DVM against baseline approaches under conventional and POLITE link adaptation. At equal delivered throughput, TDD-DVM with POLITE keeps the packet failure ratio of the full drain voltage while consuming up to 35% less power than it under conventional link adaptation and up to 7% less than it under POLITE, roughly half of the gain of an idealized reference.

title: Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
abstract: While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $Δ^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.

title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.

title: Shear viscosity from complex light-cone expansion
abstract: Near thermal equilibrium, the transverse momentum density in a fluid diffuses according to $ω(k) \sim - i {\cal D} k^2$ at small $k$, where the diffusion coefficient ${\cal D}$ is proportional to the shear viscosity. In field theories with a holographic dual description in terms of classical gravity, the shear-mode frequency $ω(k)$ approaches the light cone at large imaginary wave vector. We develop a WKB approach to study this limit. For black branes in AdS$_{p+2}$, we determine the leading terms of the asymptotic large-$k$ expansion of the shear-mode frequency $ω(k)$. In the case of AdS$_{5}$, we compute a large number of terms of this series and use resummation techniques to analytically continue the result to small $k$. We find strong evidence that $ω(k)$ is analytic at $k=0$ and vanishes there, which amounts to the existence of hydrodynamics encoded in the large-$k$ physics. Taking 10 terms in the large-$k$ expansion of $ω(k)$ gives an answer for ${\cal D}$ which is accurate to better than $0.5\%$.

title: From entropy waves to vortex sheets for the Euler equations
abstract: We construct piecewise smooth solutions of the full compressible Euler equations that evolve from entropy waves into vortex sheets while retaining a strictly positive Taylor jump. For every integer $κ\geq1$, we obtain solutions satisfying initial material compatibility for pressure and velocity through order $κ$, whose tangential velocity jump has a nonzero leading term of order $t^{κ+1}$. These solutions are periodic in the tangential variables and admit a smooth realization in a slab with impermeable walls. We also construct solutions on a local nonperiodic tangential patch that satisfy initial material compatibility at every order, yet have a tangential velocity jump that is nonzero for every sufficiently small positive time and flat at $t=0$. The finite-order construction uses a normal Cauchy-Kowalevski problem for velocity potentials, whereas the all-order construction uses a homogeneous reduction to a smooth hyperbolic Cauchy problem.

title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.

title: Time-temperature superposition from multi-temperature chirp rheometry of thermorheologically simple materials via physics-informed Gaussian processes
abstract: Inferring constitutive laws from transient response data is a central inverse problem in soft condensed-matter physics, particularly when the relevant relaxation spectrum extends beyond the time window of a single experiment. Time-temperature superposition (TTS) constrains this problem for thermorheologically simple materials in the linear viscoelastic regime by allowing temperature to rescale the characteristic relaxation time without changing the underlying shape of the relaxation spectrum. We incorporate this constraint into a physics-informed machine-learning framework for time-resolved mechanical spectroscopy via chirp rheometry. We encode compact fractional viscoelastic models as causal convolutional features derived from the Boltzmann superposition principle, and we jointly fit multi-temperature chirp records using sparse variational Gaussian process regression. The model infers horizontal shift factors, constitutive parameters, and an observational-noise scale directly from time-domain stress-strain signals measured in the linear viscoelastic regime, without first extracting frequency-domain spectra or manually shifting separate curves. For synthetic Fractional Maxwell data, the method recovers the generating constitutive law from a prescribed model library and latent shifts over stress-noise levels from 3% to 25%. Applied to a DGEBA-IPDA epoxy dataset spanning the glass-transition regime, the pooled likelihood distinguishes competing fractional rheology models using the Bayesian information criterion. These results recast TTS master-curve construction as probabilistic inference over latent time rescaling and linear viscoelasticity, while also identifying limitations, such as homoscedastic noise and weakly informative spectral regimes.

title: A classical trajectory method for diatom-atom-atom ternary association reactions
abstract: We introduce a classical trajectory method for calculating direct diatom-atom-atom ternary association re- action rates that incorporates the rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic reactant. By treating the diatomic molecule as a rigid rotor, we include the effects of the anisotropy of the molecule-atom interaction and the dynamical effects of the rotational motion. We apply this approach to a system of experimental interest, CD+ + He + He, along with the isotopic variant CH+ + He + He -> CHHe+ + He, and examine the role of the internal, rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic molecule. In particular, we find that in the regime where the collision energy is much smaller than the rotational energy of the entrance channel, the rotational motion leads to deviation from the classical threshold law by violating the assumptions of long-range capture theory models.

title: Linear transformations of tropical matrices preserving individual values of the cyclicity index
abstract: The cyclicity index is used to study the periodic behavior of powers of tropical matrices. It is determined by the structure of the critical subgraph of a matrix, which consists of the cycles with the largest average weight. In this paper bijective linear transformations of tropical matrices that preserve an individual value $k\neq 2$ of this invariant are studied.

title: Polyhedral RIS Architecture with Quantum-Assisted Facet Selection for Uniform Coverage
abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) direct coverage toward moving user equipment (UE), but practical deployments involve discrete phase control, uncertain facet positions, and UE mobility, which require the problem to be re-solved continually. We consider these challenges for the chamfered hexagonal polyhedral RIS, which provides nearly uniform coverage. With both incidence and departure angles, we bound in closed form the gain loss of its best facet relative to the best possible reflecting facet, include the known b-bit quantization loss, and extend the bound to joint random mounting errors of all facets. For a precoded multi-user downlink, each facet-selection subproblem of the max-min rate design is shown to be an exact quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, suited to repeated time-constrained solving. The deployment of the base station in relation to the RIS allows the polyhedral surface to bring down the percentage of dead zones in vertical planar panels from 77% to 0.3% and increase the minimum rate by 34% relative to the STAR panel. The simulated annealing algorithm finds the optimum solution in 95% of the cases. The quantum approximation algorithm fails to do so.

title: Variance of relative entropy over random states
abstract: Average relative entropy over major generic random states is recently studied. In this work, the investigation is extended by deriving the variances of relative entropy over the Hilbert--Schmidt and Bures--Hall ensembles, which characterize its fluctuations around the average value. Exact results for the variances of relative entropy between independent states drawn from the same ensemble and from two different ensembles are obtained. These results further indicate that the average relative entropy is typical in the considered limiting regimes. In addition to the matrix-level calculations similar to the average relative entropy, eigenvalue correlation functions of the ensembles are involved in the variance computations through the use of zonal polynomials.

title: Rank 3 curve semistable Higgs bundles: the nilpotent case
abstract: A Higgs bundle on a smooth complex projective variety is curve semistable if its pullback to every smooth projective curve is semistable. A 2008 conjecture asserts that this is equivalent to slope semistability for some polarization plus vanishing discriminant. One direction is known, the converse holds in rank two, and Huang recently gave a rank-four counterexample. We prove the conjecture for rank three nilpotent Higgs bundles in any dimension. We treat separately the two possible cases: if the Higgs field $ϕ$ is nilpotent of order two, there is a divisorial component of a Higgs Grassmannian where nefness of the normalized tautological class forces the discriminant to vanish; otherwise, $ϕ$ is regular nilpotent, and then the canonical kernel flag, commutativity and Bogomolov's lemma on line subbundles of the cotangent bundle complete the proof.

title: Configuration-Independent Low-Energy Gaps in Graphene Nanoribbons: A $δ$-Scatterer Transfer-Matrix Approach
abstract: Transport measurements on lithographically patterned graphene nanoribbons suggest that the gap depends primarily on ribbon width rather than on crystallographic edge orientation, in contrast to predictions of ideal tight-binding models. To address this, we develop a transfer-matrix approach, based on the theory of finite periodic systems, in which each carbon atom of the honeycomb lattice is represented by an individual $δ$-scatterer with interaction strength $γ^{}_δ$ and the nanoribbon is treated as a confined multichannel finite periodic system. We derive the unit-cell transfer matrix for both arm-chair and zig-zag edge configurations and obtain the transmission and channel-coupling coefficients in closed form. The transmission spectra display the resonant band structure characteristic of finite periodic systems, with the number of resonances per allowed band increasing with the number of unit cells. For $γ_δ=0$ the ribbons are fully transparent; for $γ_δ>0$ a low-energy transport gap opens and grows linearly with the scatterer strength, $Δ=0.364265\,γ_δ$, identically for arm-chair and zig-zag edges. These results are consistent with the reported absence of a systematic dependence on orientation, while the analytical results show that interchannel coupling vanishes exactly for arm-chair ribbons and decreases with increasing width for zig-zag ribbons, revealing the role of edge geometry. Together, these findings indicate that atomic-scale scattering, represented by the $δ$-potential formalism, provides a common orientation-independent contribution to the low-energy transport gap in the pristine ribbons considered here.

title: EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.

title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces
abstract: Organic molecules are versatile building blocks for the formation of complex low-dimensional nanostructures on surfaces. Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we systematically compare the properties of isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me$_6$) molecules on three different surfaces: metallic Au(111), a semiconducting ferromagnetic monolayer of FeCl$_2$, and a cleaved superconducting surface of bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$. We show that STS and DFT alone are insufficient to quantify charge transfer for these cases. Instead, we complement these methods with Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements and model Hamiltonian calculations to demonstrate that on Au(111) and FeCl$_2$, Me$_6$ molecules donate a single electron to the substrate, whereas on NbSe$_2$ two electrons are transferred from molecule to substrate. Our work provides insight into the interplay of charge transfer, screening, and molecule-substrate coupling, and develops experimental and theoretical methods for comparing the properties of adsorbates across different surfaces for future studies.

title: Single-molecule cold chemistry: Isotopic branching ratios of the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction at cryogenic temperatures
abstract: Isotopic branching in ion-molecule reactions influences interstellar deuterium fractionation, yet its dynamics remain poorly understood for many important systems at astrophysically relevant temperatures. Here, we investigate H- and D-atom transfer in the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction using single sympathetically cooled water ions in a cryogenic radiofrequency trap. Nondestructive identification of the products from 441 individual reaction events at a mean collision energy of 7 K reveals an $\mathrm{H_3O^+/H_2DO^+}$ product branching ratio of $1.50 \pm 0.15$ demonstrating a preferential H-atom transfer. The experiments are rationalized using quasi-classical-trajectory calculations which indicate a transition from direct dynamics at higher energies to a complex-mediated reaction under the present experimental conditions and point to an important role of intramolecular vibrational redistribution affecting the isotopic branching in this regime. The present results extend measurements into an astrochemically relevant energy regime and establish cryogenic single-ion chemistry as a new platform for resolving competing reaction pathways.

title: Combining Simulations and Spectroscopy to Design Protective Coatings on Sulfide Solid Electrolytes
abstract: Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high Li-ion conductivity and favorable processability, but their practical use is limited by electrochemical instability and moisture-induced degradation. Molecular surface coatings offer a scalable strategy to improve humidity tolerance and interfacial stability, yet there is limited understanding of the molecular-level factors governing surface interactions. By combining large-scale atomistic simulations enabled by a machine-learning potential with targeted experiments, we present a comprehensive framework for designing molecular coatings on Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (LPSCl). Using a PET-MAD interatomic potential fine-tuned on an r$^2$SCAN reference dataset covering LPSCl surfaces, molecular adsorbates, and their interactions, we model surface adsorption of carboxylic (CA), sulfonic (SA), and phosphonic (PA) acids with alkyl chains of varying lengths and the interaction of these coated surfaces with water at finite temperature. The simulations show that lithiated head groups generally exhibit more favorable adsorption energies. Impedance spectroscopy shows that the lithiated coatings maintain 40--55\% of the initial ionic conductivity after powder processing. While adsorption strength is largely controlled by head-group chemistry and lithiation state, coating morphology depends primarily on alkyl-chain length and surface coverage. In particular, long-chain lithiated carboxylates form dense, brush-like hydrophobic layers that reduce water access to reactive Li surface sites, with protection setting in at a coating thickness of approximately 0.8 nm. Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

title: The ALMA Survey of Gas Evolution of PROtoplanetary disks (AGE-PRO): Evolution of dust properties from multi-wavelength observations
abstract: Understanding the evolution of solids in protoplanetary discs is important to comprehend the formation of giant planets cores and terrestrial planets. The ALMA Large Program AGE-PRO studied key disc properties in a survey of 30 protoplanetary discs across three evolutionary stages: the embedded phase (0.5-1 Myr), the middle-age phase (1-3 Myr), and the end of the disc lifetime (2-6 Myr). Preliminary dust properties were estimated using 1.3 mm observations, but a multi-wavelength analysis provides a better constraint of important properties such as the dust disc mass, the dust temperature, and the maximum grain size. We present new ALMA 3.1 mm and 1.5 mm (Bands 3 and 5) continuum observations of the complete survey of 30 AGE-PRO discs. We fitted the observed visibilities and derived radial brightness profiles, spatially resolving 20 discs from the AGE-PRO sample at the two studied wavelengths. A multi-wavelength modelling was performed including also the radial profiles from the 1.3 mm observations. Our results replicate trends obtained from the single wavelength analysis: the dust disc size seems to be constant over age and the dust disc mass decreases with time, with a factor $\sim$10-40 uncertainty from opacity assumptions. This result implies much lower gas-to-dust mass ratios for the discs in our sample than previously reported. In addition, the derived spectral indices are consistent with optically thick emission in a large fraction of the AGE-PRO discs, in particular for the Ophiuchus and Lupus discs.

title: A Highly Efficient Depth-Averaged Material Point Method for Geophysical Mass Flows
abstract: Probabilistic hazard assessment of geophysical mass flows requires large simulation ensembles and thus fast and robust numerical models. We present an open-source depth-averaged material point method formulated in global Cartesian coordinates, using Lagrangian particles to track the flow margin. A separate basal friction step based on the Coulomb, Voellmy, or $μ(I)$-rheology brings the flow to rest without artificial stopping criteria. Our model reproduces analytical solutions for a sliding block and dam-break problems and matches the deposit of a laboratory granular column collapse. A back-calculation of the 2023 Brienz/Brinzauls rockslide (Switzerland) at 1m resolution (190'000 particles) runs faster than real time on a single CPU core. Calibrated to the observed runout, the three friction laws yield very similar results, but Coulomb friction shows a slightly wider affected area than Voellmy and $μ(I)$. A probabilistic 1632-simulation ensemble at 5m resolution was computed in 76s. The model is one to two orders of magnitude faster than established depth-averaged models used in engineering practice, making catchment-style ensemble simulations feasible on a desktop computer.

title: Nonclassicality from Incomplete Fock-State Statistics
abstract: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. The method contains known analytical criteria as special cases while generally detecting substantially larger nonclassical regions. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms. As a case study, we apply it to the resonant Jaynes--Cummings model with thermal states and reveal nonclassicality at short interaction times and close to thermal balance, where detection of nonclassicality is otherwise challenging.

title: HoloBoxing: A Simple Recipe for Humanoid Boxing with 7 Minutes of Single-GPU Training
abstract: HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.

title: Recommender regret for improving regularised RL estimation with bandits and MCTS
abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms rely on estimators, like Monte Carlo tree search or one-step look-ahead, to provide policy, value, or Q-value estimates in training and inference. However, existing bandit-based estimation frameworks evaluate sampling efficiency, not the quality of estimates. We address this by formalising estimate generation as a recommendation process, treating bandit-based sampling as an improvement operator. To evaluate the quality of a recommendation (estimate), we define regulariser-aware recommender regrets, analysing their lower bounds, and proving that simple algorithms like uniform sampling can achieve these bounds. Finally, we unify bandit- and search-based target improvement under recommender MCTS. Across synthetic trees, arcade games, and scientific discovery tasks, recommenders often yield faster target convergence and superior downstream performance. Our experiments characterise for the first time the potential of regularised MCTS in scientific applications.

title: Classical, Machine Learning, and Hybrid Solvers for Partial Differential Equations: An Evidence-Weighted Review and Decision Framework
abstract: Machine learning for partial differential equations raises a practical question: when are classical, learned, or hybrid solvers justified? This survey compares the three families in a decision framework organized by data availability, query volume, and certification needs. An amortization law, tested on parametric Darcy flow, shows that surrogates trained on solver-generated data break even only after many queries, beyond thirty thousand for errors below one percent. An evidence ladder, a benchmark reanalysis, and three case studies show that claims of speedup and generalization carry the weakest evidence. Solver choice should follow regime, query volume, and evidence quality, not method novelty.

title: Folding of Free Polymers Under Confinement by Responsive Hydrogels
abstract: Controlling the folding of biopolymers in crowded and confined environments, such as the interior of biological cells, remains a significant challenge. Macromolecular crowding and spatial confinement can strongly influence transition pathways between folded and unfolded states of proteins. Such environments can be mimicked in experiments by confining polymers within soft, tunable media, such as hydrogels -- cross-linked polymer networks that swell by absorbing solvent and exhibit stimulus-dependent responsiveness. Here, we develop a self-consistent mean-field theory for the equilibrium swelling and internal composition of a hydrogel immersed in a solution of free polymer coils. The theory extends the Flory-Rehner framework by incorporating free polymer coils, modeled as fluctuating ellipsoids, whose sizes and shapes are characterized by the eigenvalues of the gyration tensor. Confinement of the coils within gel pores is characterized by an effective free-volume fraction, parametrized from numerical calculations for self-avoiding-walk chains between hard walls. Coupled chemical potential equilibrium conditions are solved numerically over ranges of coil molecular weight and free polymer concentration. We find that free polymers drive a non-monotonic swelling response of hydrogels, with osmotic swelling at low concentrations followed by deswelling at higher concentrations, in qualitative agreement with experiment. We further demonstrate that confinement within gel pores reduces the radius of gyration and asphericity of embedded polymer coils, driving them toward compact, globular conformations analogous to folded protein states. These results establish a theoretical foundation for using responsive hydrogels as tunable, artificial chaperone-like systems capable of inducing and controlling biopolymer folding.

title: Complete Multi-Band Structural Characterization for 10 Million Galaxies in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey using Deep Learning
abstract: Galaxy structure is wavelength-dependent, as different photometric bands trace distinct stellar populations and structural components. We present per-galaxy Bayesian posterior distributions of the bulge-to-total light ratio ($L_B/L_T$), effective radius ($R_e$), and flux ($F$) in the $g$, $r$, and $i$ bands for nearly $10$ million galaxies across $\sim$1400\,deg$^2$ of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) Wide survey at $z \leq 0.75$ and $m < 23$. To our knowledge, this is the largest multi-band catalog of bulge--disk structural parameters with per-galaxy posteriors. $\sim$3.9 million of the above galaxies have full multi-band coverage. Measurements are generated using the Galaxy Morphology Posterior Estimation Network (\gampen{}), a Bayesian deep-learning framework. We demonstrate that we can adapt \gampen{} from previously-trained single-band models to the new bands by using transfer learning on only $\sim$0.5\% of our dataset. Despite this extremely small training set, \gampen{} successfully reproduces light-profile fitting measurements and its output posteriors are extremely well-calibrated with $\lesssim6\%$ mean deviation. This approach offers a scalable pathway to structural parameter measurements with robust uncertainties for Rubin, Euclid, and Roman data, which we will pursue in forthcoming work. While structural measurements remain robust across most bands and redshift ranges, performance degrades significantly for the $g$-band at $z \gtrsim 0.5$, where it increasingly probes rest-frame ultraviolet emission; these measurements are therefore excluded from the public release. This public catalog will enable large-scale statistical studies of morphological color gradients, wavelength-dependent galaxy structure, and galaxy evolution.

title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control
abstract: Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer-Burmeister reformulation and a primal-dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet .

title: What Mean Error Misses: Device-Clock Diagnostics for Evaluating Eye Tracking across Three Virtual Reality Headsets
abstract: Gaze research in virtual reality needs eye trackers of known error. Thirty participants completed the same protocol on the Meta Quest Pro (QP), HTC VIVE Pro Eye (PE) and HTC VIVE Focus Vision (FV); to our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of the FV eye tracker. In a random-saccade task, median participant mean error was 1.04° on QP, 1.50° on PE and 2.41° on FV, which remained least accurate after linear recalibration. In a later block with a darker background, PE error rose by 0.70°. FV samples were positively correlated: dispersion was 9.8 times the sample-to-sample root mean square. The device clocks showed losses that mean error hides. QP paused for up to 6.04 s, and FV skipped single samples. During instructed eye closures, QP flagged every sample valid while gaze moved 9.74°. Evaluations should report repeated timestamps, loss composition on the device clock and validity during eye closures.

title: A Population Synthesis Model for Odd Radio Circles Produced by Shock-Bubble Interactions
abstract: Odd Radio Circles (ORCs) are edge-brightened rings of diffuse radio emission of roughly arcminute size whose physical origin remains debated. One proposed mechanism is vortex formation through Shock-Bubble interaction (SBI), in which a merger or accretion shock re-energizes a fossil radio lobe into an edge-brightened ring. We test whether this mechanism can reproduce the observed ORC abundance using a Monte Carlo population-synthesis model that combines the galaxy stellar mass function, the radio-AGN incidence relation, dark-matter halo merger histories, and the inflation and buoyant survival of AGN-inflated bubbles, with synthetic radio fluxes and ring geometries drawn from a grid of magnetohydrodynamic SBI simulations. Applying survey-specific selection to the ASKAP-EMU Pilot Survey (944 MHz) and the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS; 144 MHz), we predict $2.7^{+3.9}_{-1.6}$ detectable ORCs in the EMU Pilot, matching the three found there, and $268^{+331}_{-148}$ in LoTSS, of which $7.5^{+9.5}_{-4.2}$ have a counterpart at 1.4 GHz. The predicted hosts are mostly central galaxies in group-scale halos. The predicted rings are physically smaller and lie at lower redshifts than the galaxies identified as hosts of the known ORCs, suggesting that SBI produces mainly the nearby part of the ORC population, or that some ORCs are associated with the wrong host. The population synthesis model also predicts a large population of low surface brightness steep-spectrum ORCs in the LoTSS band, implying a large hidden population and predicting that deeper low-frequency surveys should uncover many more ORCs than are currently known. These results indicate that shock-bubble interactions can account for at least part of the observed incidence of ORCs.

title: Stationary bistable fronts on a periodic necklace graph: existence, stability and multiplicity
abstract: We study stationary fronts for a bistable reaction-diffusion equation with the McKean reaction on a periodic necklace metric graph. For profiles that agree on each pair of parallel edges, the problem reduces to a scalar equation on the real line with a periodic, piecewise constant diffusion coefficient. The diffusion contrast of the necklace is not small, so the coefficient cannot be treated as a small perturbation of a constant. Because the McKean reaction is piecewise linear, the equation is affine between threshold crossings and coefficient interfaces, and a front is determined explicitly by its crossing points. We find an explicit interval of reaction thresholds, the pinning interval, such that stationary fronts, monotone or not, exist exactly for thresholds in this interval. Up to translations by the spatial period, there are exactly two decreasing fronts at each interior threshold and one front at each endpoint. For each fixed interior threshold, one decreasing front is Lyapunov stable and the other is unstable in the $W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ norm, among mild solutions with one continuously moving threshold crossing. The crossing phases of the two decreasing fronts also determine nonmonotone fronts. For each interior threshold and odd $m\geq3$, choose $m$ periods of the coefficient that are sufficiently far apart. There are then exactly $2^m$ fronts with one threshold crossing in each chosen period and none elsewhere. Varying the chosen periods gives infinitely many inequivalent fronts with $m$ crossings.

title: CO2-Induced Shifts in the Confined Phase Transformation of CH4 in Metal-Organic Frameworks
abstract: A sharp increase in gas uptake over a narrow pressure range can occur for fluids confined in nanoporous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), reflecting a transformation between distinct adsorption states, often accompanied by the existence of metastable states. Understanding how co-adsorbed species modify this behavior is important for predicting and optimizing gas storage and separation. Here, we investigate the effect of CO2 on the adsorption transformation of confined CH4 in rigid IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8. Transition-Matrix Monte Carlo (TMMC) simulations were performed for systems containing 0-75 and 0-150 CO2 molecules in IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8, respectively. While the addition of CO2 decreases the maximum CH4 uptake, consistent with competition for pore space, remarkably, the presence of CO2 significantly shifts the discontinuity in the CH4 adsorption isotherm to substantially lower pressures relative to the pure CH4 system. This promotion of the high-density CH4 phase at lower pressures demonstrates that CO2 substantially alters the thermodynamic landscape governing confined CH4 through changes in both fluid-fluid and fluid-framework interactions. These results establish CO2 as a thermodynamic modifier of confined CH4 behavior and suggest that controlled co-adsorption provides a means of tuning adsorption transformations in nanoporous materials.

title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq

title: Hot Spots: From Smooth to Nonsmooth Simply Connected Planar Domains
abstract: Assuming the absence of interior local extrema for first positive Neumann eigenfunctions on bounded smooth simply connected planar domains, as reported in \cite{SmoothInput}, we extend the hot spots conclusion to simply connected domains of finite area with compact Sobolev embedding and simple first positive Neumann eigenvalue. The supremum and infimum are approached in arbitrarily thin boundary layers. For bounded domains and eigenfunctions continuous up to the boundary, both extrema are attained on the boundary. We also transfer polynomial Neumann heat-kernel bounds uniformly along a conformal exhaustion and construct explicit bounded and unbounded examples, including domains with cusps and a domain with infinitely many corners and bottlenecks. Some of these examples admit no polynomial Neumann heat-kernel bound.

title: Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora
abstract: Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance.

title: A direct proof of the equivalence of the A2 and the Helson--Szego conditions
abstract: We give a direct proof of the equivalence between the Muckenhoupt $\mathcal{A}_2$ and the Helson--Szegő conditions on the unit circle $T$. A positive weight $w$ belongs to $\mathcal{A}_2(T)$ if and only if $\log w=u+Hv$, where $u,v$ are real bounded functions, $\|v\|_\infty<\fracπ{2}$, and $H$ denotes the periodic Hilbert transform. The classical proof combines the Helson--Szegő theorem with the Hunt--Muckenhoupt--Wheeden characterization of weighted boundedness of the Hilbert transform. Our proof derives the Helson--Szegő representation directly from the Muckenhoupt $\mathcal{A}_2$ condition, without using boundedness of $H$ on $L^2(w)$.

title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.

title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.

title: On the Expressive Power of Hook-Indexed State Comprehending State in the React UI Library
abstract: React is currently the most popular JavaScript library for front-end web development. It endows UI components with state via the useState construct, through a mechanism that we name hook-indexed state. However, React's implementation of hook-indexed state is both fragile and poorly understood. Programmers frequently experience unexpected behavior, and the benefits of programming in this paradigm are wholly unclear. We define Lambda-React-Hook, a core calculus that captures the essence of hook-indexed state, and give it a type system to statically rule out unexpected behavior. We then translate Lambda-React-Hook into a calculus Lambda-React-Ref based on ML-style references, and prove that this translation preserves typability and semantics, thus showing that hook-indexed state is expressible in terms of standard references. The translation is local and admits a compositional definition, but involves significant code duplication. As well as illuminating the essence of state in React, our observations can inform the design of future reactive programming systems.

title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

title: Probabilistic ultraviolet renormalization of the two-dimensional Sine-Gordon model
abstract: We give a probabilistic approach to the ultraviolet renormalization of the two-dimensional Sine-Gordon model. The model is formally described by the density $\exp(α\int \mathopen{:} \cos(βX) \mathclose{:} )$, where $X$ is a log-correlated Gaussian field. Our construction applies on bounded convex domains for every particle activity $α\in\mathbb R$ and throughout the subcritical range $β^2\in[0,4)$, below the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless threshold. We apply the martingale method introduced by Lacoin, Rhodes and Vargas to two dimensions by using refined estimates based on charge conjugation symmetries. Our result extends existing constructions by treating the full subcritical regime for a broad class of covariances.

title: Vertex operator algebra realizations of untwisted Haagerup--Izumi centers
abstract: For every odd integer $N\geq3$, we construct an untwisted Haagerup--Izumi fusion category $\mathcal H_N$ on the negative spherical branch and a simple, self-contragredient, regular, $C_2$-cofinite vertex operator algebra $E_N$ of central charge $-16N$, together with an equivalence of modular fusion categories: \[ \operatorname{Rep}(E_N)\simeq Z(\mathcal H_N). \] The VOA $E_N$ is rational, has exactly $N^2+3$ irreducible modules, and is lower bounded and integer graded, with least conformal degree $-(N-1)/2$. The proof begins with a CFT-type cyclic Virasoro extension of central charge $-5N$, whose regularity we establish. Two categorical condensations recover $\mathcal H_N$, and a finite extension by shifted lattice modules removes the auxiliary pointed factor. We identify the complete ribbon modular data of $Z(\mathcal H_N)$ with $\mathrm{MD}_{-}(\mathbb Z/N;\mathbb Z/(N^2+4),b\mapsto b^2/(N^2+4))$ in the notation of Gannon--Schopieray--Yadav, for every odd $N$.

title: Extended Hydrodynamics of Planar Heisenberg Ferromagnetic Systems
abstract: Access to hydro and quasi-hydro regimes in magnetic systems is steadily increasing with the advances in fabrication of clean materials, and motivates study of hydrodynamics beyond conventional regimes and probe non-equilibrium transport. We employ the framework of extended irreversible thermodynamics which includes dynamical dissipative currents as quasi-hydro variables, and effect the modified hydrodynamic equations suitable to describe planar Heisenberg ferromagnetic systems in both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We show that the new transport coefficients and relaxation time scales introduced by quasi-hydro variables can engineer diverse combination of dispersion relations and provide control over the nature of hydrodynamic modes. For instance, we can change the diffusive energy mode into propagating one in multiple ways, including by tuning the relaxation time of magnetization current.

title: Rational Points on Affine Varieties over Finite Fields and Polygonal Number Sequences
abstract: Authors, in an earlier work, proved that prime power subsequences of the polygonal numbers corresponding to $4$, $6$, $8$, and $10$ arise naturally as the numbers of $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points of certain double Danielewski surfaces. In this work, authors generalize the previous construction and give a new family of affine varieties over finite fields such that the number of $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points of these varieties give the prime power subsequence of every polygonal number sequence.

title: One-Million-Year-Old Nascent Eclipsing Binaries in the LMC
abstract: The light curves of nascent eclipsing binaries (EBs) feature sinusoidal reflection effects as a hot B-type main-sequence (MS) primary irradiates the near side of a cool, low-mass, pre-MS companion. We obtained multi-epoch echelle spectra with the MIKE spectrograph on the 6.5m Magellan-Clay Telescope of three nascent EBs embedded in H II regions within the LMC. By fitting atmospheric models to the spectra, the primaries are found to be mid-B dwarfs (T_eff,1 = 18,600-22,800 K; M_1 = 6.8-8.5 Msun). The dynamical masses of the secondaries are only M_2 = 0.38-0.95 Msun, yielding extremely small mass ratios q = M_2/M_1 = 0.05-0.11. Unlike solar-type primaries, which exhibit a dearth of close companions with q < 0.1 known as the brown dwarf desert, massive stars can readily form with very close companions below q < 0.1. By fitting PHOEBE models to the OGLE-III light curves, we measure the secondary radii R_2 = 2.0-2.8 Rsun and temperatures T_eff,2 = 4,000 K. The pre-MS companions are located high on the Hayashi track where evolutionary models indicate ages of only 1 Myr. Their extreme youth suggests that nascent EBs formed via inward disk migration during the previous embedded protostellar phase.

title: STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
abstract: We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.

title: Yalda-Embedding: Open Development of a Competitive Persian Retrieval Model
abstract: Despite advances in multilingual text representations, effective dense retrieval for Persian remains constrained by the limited availability of language-specific training resources and compact embedding models. We present Yalda Embedding, a 595.8-million-parameter Persian retrieval model adapted from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using more than one million query-document pairs. On eight Persian retrieval tasks from FaMTEB, the model achieves the highest macro-average among the evaluated 0.6B models, scoring 0.5488 and outperforming Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and F2LLM-v2-0.6B on every task. It also approaches Qwen3-Embedding-4B, winning on four tasks, tying on one, and trailing by 0.0075 in macro-average. An incremental ablation study examines contrastive batch size, optimization stabilization, and relational knowledge distillation from F2LLM-v2-8B. Under the one-epoch training setup, contrastive fine-tuning alone yields a modest mean improvement over initialization and regressions on two tasks. The final distilled configuration improves all eight tasks over the non-distilled model, raising the mean from 0.4813 to 0.5488 without increasing inference-time model size. These gains include hard-negative evaluation tasks despite training without explicitly mined or supplied hard negatives. We release model weights, training and evaluation code, the pairwise dataset, and its teacher-embedded counterpart, enabling inspection of data composition and training procedures, independent evaluation, and reuse without repeating expensive teacher inference.

title: Runtime BiDi Structural Verification Catches Right-to-Left Layout Defects that Accessibility, Actionability, and Logical-Property Linting Miss
abstract: Bidirectional (right-to-left, RTL) layout defects arise when interfaces authored with physical directional CSS (margin-left, border-left, text-align:left) are rendered under dir="rtl" without being mirrored. Accessibility engines (axe-core), actionability engines (Playwright), and even Stylelint's current core logical-property rule fail to localise these defects. We present runtime structural invariants -- a zero-golden mode over computed style and geometry, and a bidi-conservative differential mode -- that catch them in a headless browser. On a held-out benchmark of 14 real RTL bugs reconstructed from dated fix commits in Bootstrap and Material Components Web, the detector recovers 13/14 (2 via zero-golden, 11 via the differential mode), with no false alarm on any patched version; on the actual committed historical bootstrap.rtl.css it catches 1 of 2 attempted. It reports 0 false positives on 16 negative LTR-island cases and, in both modes, on 43 unmodified real components across four design systems and three RTL architectures (rule-of-three 95% upper bound <= 7%), and it surfaced a real directional defect in the current Bulma 1.0.4. By contrast, Stylelint's core rule emits an identical 1744 warnings on Bootstrap's LTR and correct-RTL builds, pseudo-localisation detects none of the mirroring bugs, and a naive pixel mirror-and-diff reaches only F1 0.87 with a test-set-tuned threshold. The two modes are complementary: zero-golden is the sole detector of the decoration/styling-asymmetry class (5/6) but false-flags the correct logical border-inline-end, while the differential detects none of that class yet never false-alarms and is empirically exact on the block-level inset/margin class. We scope this paper to detection; repair is future work.

title: Three subpopulations of binary black holes in mass, spin magnitudes and tilts following GWTC-5
abstract: The mass and spin distributions of merging binary black holes offer clues to their formation pathways, which remain uncertain. In this work, we model the population of binary black holes using generic subpopulations with distinct mass-ratio, spin-magnitude, and spin-tilt distributions, whose relative contributions vary with primary mass. Using the 259 binary black holes in the fifth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA catalog (GWTC-5), we resolve three subpopulations with low, medium, and high spins. The low-spin population dominates for primary masses near $35 M_\odot$, contributes roughly half of the binaries for primary masses of $10 M_\odot$, and favors nearly equal mass ratios overall; its spins are consistent with both black holes having negligible spin, with a log Bayes factor of $\log_{10}B =6.1^{+0.2}_{-0.3}$ in favor of vanishing spins. The medium-spin population accounts for the other half of the population around primary masses of $10 M_\odot$ and favors spin magnitudes $χ_i \approx 0.2$ for both components, preferentially aligned orientations, and comparable mass ratios. The high-spin population dominates above primary masses of $60 M_\odot$ and also contributes at lower masses $\sim 20 M_\odot$; it favors a rapidly spinning primary ($χ_1 \approx 0.7$), a broad range of secondary spins, widely distributed spin orientations, and a broad mass-ratio distribution. Allowing for a fourth subpopulation yields no distinct additional mass-ratio or spin distribution, as it becomes degenerate with existing features. To resolve highly concentrated features in spin, we control the variance of standard Monte Carlo likelihood estimators using truncated Gaussian mixture models. Taken together, our results add to a growing body of evidence for substructure in the population of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA black holes, providing further clues to uncover their formation histories.

title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
abstract: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

title: Certain Quantum States Already Require Quantum Time Evolution
abstract: Model-independent tests of quantum theory, such as Bell inequality violations, focus on static properties of the theory and do not rely on its dynamical aspects. Hence, this core part of quantum theory remains largely untested in a model-independent way. We show that the structure of quantum time evolution can be examined by testing the consistency between the state space and the dynamical laws. Considering a class of generalized phase-space theories, we find that certain quantum states can only be part of a theory if the time evolution is quantum: their evolution in anharmonic potentials would otherwise result in unphysical, negative marginal distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of the first excited state of a quantum harmonic oscillator is already sufficient to single out the Moyal bracket (quantum dynamics) to leading order in $\hbar^2$. We outline how theory-independent Wigner tomography of this state can be used to empirically exclude nonquantum dynamical theories.

title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density
abstract: Sluggish vacancy-mediated self-diffusion in lithium metal limits the critical current density (CCD) of Li anodes in solid-state batteries by promoting interfacial void formation during stripping. To enhance the effective vacancy concentration while preserving the bcc Li host, we screen 50 substitutional solutes using density functional theory (DFT) within a funnel based on automatic phase diagram construction, solution energies, solute-vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits. Using an adaptation of the Lomer model for the dilute limit, we show that only Ag, Ge, and Cd solid solutions are predicted to reach $1~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ within their solubility limits. The thermodynamically estimated CCD of Ag at $\sim 9$ at.% reaches $\sim 4~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ at a theoretical capacity of $1522~\mathrm{mAh~g^{-1}}$. Migration barrier calculations indicate that the enhancement may be partially offset by vacancy trapping, necessitating further validation via molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, Hume-Rothery rules alone prove insufficient as prefilters, whereas machine-learning models trained on the DFT data can eliminate most unsuitable solutes early in the funnel and extend the workflow to related solid-solution searches.

title: Modified scattering for the 3D Hartree equation with singular external potentials
abstract: We establish modified scattering for the three-dimensional Hartree equation with Coulomb interaction and singular external potentials, including repulsive Coulomb and inverse-square potentials. In the defocusing case, the result holds for arbitrary initial data in $H^{0,1}(\mathbb R^3)\cap H^{1,0}(\mathbb R^3)$. In particular, we obtain large-data modified scattering for the flat defocusing Hartree equation. For the focusing problem with repulsive Coulomb potential $V(x)=κ|x|^{-1}$, we prove radial modified scattering under the sharp mass condition $|λ|\|u_0\|_2^2\leq 2κ$, including the endpoint, and construct standing waves at every larger mass. Our argument obtains strong $L^2$ convergence from rescaled energy and comparison with a frozen-field evolution.

title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time
abstract: We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $ε$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/ε$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix. On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.

title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

title: A Central Limit Theorem for the Driver Site Frequency Spectrum
abstract: We consider a supercritical two-type continuous-time linear birth-death process with mutation and selection, in which wild-type individuals give rise to mutant offspring with a larger net-growth rate. We previously had obtained first-order law of large number results for the driver site frequency spectrum. We return to obtain a second-order central limit theorem, in which we show stable convergence of a scaling of the deviation of the SFS from its first-order limit.
